metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So for instance, if you're trying to play Go,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: your experience with Go is all the Go games you've played or you've seen,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: or you've simulated in your mind, let's say,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: and your priors are things like, well, Go is a game on a 2D grid,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: and we have lots of hard-coded priors about the organization of 2D space.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And the rules of how the dynamics of this, the physics of this game in the 2D space.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And the idea that you have to, what winning is.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes, exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And other board games can also share some similarities with Go,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: and if you've played these board games, then with respect to the game of Go,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: that would be part of your priors about the game.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Well, it's interesting to think about the game of Go,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: how many priors are actually brought to the table.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: When you look at self-play, reinforcement learning-based mechanisms that do learning,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: it seems like the number of priors is pretty low.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But you're saying you should be...

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: There is a 2D special priors in the Covenant.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Right. But you should be clear at making those priors explicit.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes. So in particular, I think if your goal is to measure a human-like form of intelligence,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: then you should clearly establish that you want the AI you're testing

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: to start from the same set of priors that humans start with.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Right. So, I mean, to me personally, but I think to a lot of people,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: the human side of things is very interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So testing intelligence for humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: What do you think is a good test of human intelligence?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Well, that's the question that psychometrics is interested in.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: There's an entire subfield of psychology that deals with this question.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So what's psychometrics?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Psychometrics is the subfield of psychology that tries to measure, quantify aspects of the human mind,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: so in particular, cognitive abilities, intelligence, and personality traits as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So, like, what are...

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It might be a weird question, but what are, like, the first principles of psychometrics that it operates on?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: What are the priors it brings to the table?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So it's a field with a fairly long history.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So, you know, psychology sometimes gets a bad reputation for not having very reproducible results,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: and some psychometrics has actually some fairly solidly reproducible results.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So the ideal goals of the field is, you know, a test should be reliable,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: which is a notion tied to reproducibility.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It should be valid, meaning that it should actually measure what you say it measures.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So, for instance, if you're saying that you're measuring intelligence,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: then your test results should be correlated with things that you expect to be correlated with intelligence,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: like success in school or success in the workplace and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It should be standardized, meaning that you can administer your test to many different people in the same conditions,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: and it should be free from bias, meaning that, for instance, if your test involves the English language,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: then you have to be aware that this creates a bias against people who have English as their second language

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: or people who can't speak English at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So, of course, these principles for creating psychometric tests are very much nigh-to-all.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I don't think every psychometric test is really either reliable, valid, or free from bias,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: but at least the field is aware of these weaknesses and is trying to address them.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So, it's kind of interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Ultimately, you're only able to measure, like you said previously, the skill,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: but you're trying to do a bunch of measures of different skills that correlate, as you mentioned,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: strongly with some general concept of cognitive ability.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes, yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So, what's the G-factor?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So, right, there are many different kinds of tests of intelligence,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: and each of them is interested in different aspects of intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Some of them will deal with language, some of them will deal with spatial vision,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: maybe mental rotations, numbers, and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: When you run these very different tests at scale, what you start seeing is that there are clusters of correlations among test results.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So, for instance, if you look at homework at school,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: you will see that people who do well at math are also likely statistically to do well in physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And what's more, people who do well at math and physics are also statistically likely to do well in things that sound completely unrelated,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: like writing an English essay, for instance.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And so, when you see clusters of correlations in statistical terms, you would explain them with a latent variable.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And the latent variable that would, for instance, explain the relationship between being good at math and being good at physics would be cognitive ability.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And the G-factor is the latent variable that explains the fact that every test of intelligence that you can come up with results on this test and end up being correlated.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So, there is some single unique variable that explains these correlations. That's the G-factor.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So, it's a statistical construct. It's not really something you can directly measure, for instance, in a person.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But it's there.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But it's there. It's there at scale. And that's also one thing I want to mention about psychometrics.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: When you talk about measuring intelligence in humans, for instance, some people get a little bit worried. They will say, that sounds dangerous.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Maybe that sounds potentially discriminatory and so on. And they're not wrong.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And the thing is, personally, I'm not interested in psychometrics as a way to characterize one individual person.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Like, if I get your psychometric personality assessment or your IQ, I don't think that actually tells me much about you as a person.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think psychometrics is most useful as a statistical tool. So, it's most useful at scale.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's most useful when you start getting test results for a large number of people and you start cross-correlating these test results.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Because that gives you information about the structure of the human mind, in particular, about the structure of human cognitive abilities.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So, at scale, psychometrics paints a certain picture of the human mind. And that's interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that's what's relevant to AI, the structure of human cognitive abilities.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah, it gives you an insight into it. I mean, to me, I remember when I learned about G-factor, it seemed like it would be impossible for it to be real, even as a statistical variable.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It felt kind of like astrology. It's like wishful thinking among psychologists.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But the more I learned, I realized that there's some... I mean, I'm not sure what to make about human beings, the fact that the G-factor is a thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That there's a commonality across all of human species, that there does seem to be a strong correlation between cognitive abilities.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That's kind of fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah. So, human cognitive abilities have a structure.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: The most mainstream theory of the structure of cognitive abilities is called CHC theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's Cattle, Horn, Carol. It's the name of the three psychologists who contributed key pieces of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And it describes cognitive abilities as a hierarchy with three levels.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And at the top, you have the G-factor. Then you have broad cognitive abilities, for instance, through the intelligence, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That encompass a broad set of possible kinds of tasks that are all related.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And then you have narrow cognitive abilities at the last level, which is closer to task-specific skill.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And there are actually different theories of the structure of cognitive abilities that just emerge from different statistical analysis of IQ test results.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But they all describe a hierarchy with a kind of G-factor at the top.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And you're right that the G-factor is not quite real in the sense that it's not something you can observe and measure, like your height, for instance.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But it's really in the sense that you see it in a statistical analysis of the data, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: One thing I want to mention is that the fact that there is a G-factor does not really mean that human intelligence is, in general, in a strong sense, does not mean human intelligence can be applied to any problem at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that someone who has a high IQ is going to be able to solve any problem at all. That's not quite what it means, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: One popular analogy to understand it is the sports analogy.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: If you consider the concept of physical fitness, it's a concept that's very similar to intelligence because it's a useful concept.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's something you can intuitively understand. Some people are fit, maybe like you. Some people are not as fit, maybe like me.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But none of us can fly.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Absolutely.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's constrained to our specific set of skills.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: If you're very fit, that doesn't mean you can do anything at all in any environment.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You obviously cannot fly. You cannot survive at the bottom of the ocean and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And if you were a scientist and you wanted to precisely define and measure physical fitness in humans, then you would come up with a battery of tests.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You would have running 100 meters, playing soccer, playing table tennis, swimming, and so on. And if you ran these tests over many different people, you would start seeing correlations in test results.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: For instance, people who are good at soccer are also good at sprinting.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And you would explain these correlations with physical abilities that are strictly analogous to cognitive abilities.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And then you would start also observing correlations between biological characteristics, like maybe lung volume is correlated with being a fast runner, for instance.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: In the same way that there are neurophysical correlates of cognitive abilities.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And at the top of the hierarchy of physical abilities that you would be able to observe, you would have a G factor, a physical G factor, which would map to physical fitness.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And as you just said, that doesn't mean that people with high physical fitness can fly. It doesn't mean human morphology and human physiology is universal.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's actually super specialized. We can only do the things that we were evolved to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: We are not appropriate to... You could not exist on Venus or Mars or in the void of space, but on the ocean.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So that said, one thing that's really striking and remarkable is that our morphology generalizes far beyond the environments that we evolved for.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Like in a way you could say we evolved to run after prey in the savanna, right? That's very much where our human morphology comes from.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that said, we can do a lot of things that are completely unrelated to that. We can climb mountains. We can swim across lakes.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: We can play table tennis. I mean, table tennis is very different from what we were evolved to do, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So our morphology, our bodies, our sense and motor affordances have a degree of generality that is absolutely remarkable.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And I think cognition is very similar to that. Our cognitive abilities have a degree of generality that goes far beyond what the mind was initially supposed to do,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: which is why we can play music and write novels and go to Mars and do all kinds of crazy things.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But it's not universal in the same way that human morphology and our body is not appropriate for actually most of the universe by volume.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: In the same way, you could say that the human mind is not really appropriate for most of potential problem space by volume.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So we have very strong cognitive biases, actually, that mean that there are certain types of problems that we handle very well

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: and certain types of problems that we are completely inadapted for. So that's really how we interpret the G factor.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's not a sign of strong generality. It's really just the broadest cognitive ability.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But our abilities, whether we are talking about sensory motor abilities or cognitive abilities, they remain very specialized in the human condition.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Within the constraints of the human cognition, they're general.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes, absolutely.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But the constraints, as you're saying, are very limited.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So we evolved our cognition and our body evolved in very specific environments.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Because our environment was so variable, fast changing and so unpredictable, part of the constraints that drove our evolution is generality itself.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So we were in a way evolved to be able to improvise in all kinds of physical or cognitive environments.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And for this reason, it turns out that the minds and bodies that we ended up with can be applied to much, much broader scope than what they were evolved for.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that's truly remarkable. And that's a degree of generalization that is far beyond anything you can see in artificial systems today.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That said, it does not mean that human intelligence is anywhere universal.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah, it's not general.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You know, it's a kind of exciting topic for people even outside of artificial intelligence IQ tests.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think it's Mensa, whatever. There's different degrees of difficulty for questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: We talked about this offline a little bit too about sort of difficult questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You know, what makes a question on an IQ test more difficult or less difficult?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Do you think? So the thing to keep in mind is that there's no such thing as a question that's intrinsically difficult.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It has to be difficult to suspect to the things you already know and the things you can already do.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So in terms of an IQ test question, typically it would be structured, for instance, as a set of demonstration input and output pairs.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And then you would be given a test input, a prompt, and you would need to recognize or produce the corresponding output.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And in that narrow context, you could say a difficult question is a question where the input prompt is very surprising and unexpected, given the training examples.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Just even the nature of the patterns that you're observing in the input prompt.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: For instance, let's say you have a rotation problem. You must rotate the shape by 90 degrees.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: If I give you two examples and then I give you one prompt, which is actually one of the two training examples, then there is zero generalization difficulty for the task.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's actually a trivial task. You just recognize that it's one of the training examples and you produce the same answer.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Now, if it's a more complex shape, there is a little bit more generalization, but it remains that you are still doing the same thing at test time as you were being demonstrated at training time.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: A difficult task is a task that will require some amount of test time adaptation, some amount of improvisation.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So consider, I don't know, you're teaching a class on quantum physics or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: If you wanted to test the understanding that students have of the material, you would come up with an exam that's very different from anything they've seen on the internet when they were cramming.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: On the other hand, if you wanted to make it easy, you would just give them something that's very similar to the mock exams that they've taken, something that's just a simple interpolation of questions that they've already seen.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And so that would be an easy exam. It's very similar to what you've been trained on.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And a difficult exam is one that really probes your understanding because it forces you to improvise. It forces you to do things that are different from what you were exposed to before.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So that said, it doesn't mean that the exam that requires improvisation is intrinsically hard, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Because maybe you're a quantum physics expert, so when you take the exam, this is actually stuff that despite being new to the students, it's not new to you.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So it can only be difficult with respect to what the test taker already knows and with respect to the information that the test taker has about the task.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So that's what I mean by controlling for priors, what the information brings to the table and the experience, which is the trained data.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So in the case of the quantum physics exam, that would be all the course material itself and all the mock exams that students might have taken online.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah, it's interesting because I've also sent you an email and asked you, this is just this curious question of what's a really hard IQ test question.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And I've been talking to also people who have designed IQ tests. There's a few folks on the Internet. It's like a thing. People are really curious about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And people, most of the IQ tests they designed, they religiously protect against the correct answers.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You can't find the correct answers anywhere. In fact, the question is ruined once you know even the approach you're supposed to take.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That said, the approach is implicit in the training examples. So if you release the training examples, it's over.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Which is why in ARC, for instance, there is a test set that is private and no one has seen it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: No, for really tough IQ questions, it's not obvious. It's not because the ambiguity.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I mean, we have to look to them, but some number sequences and so on, it's not completely clear.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So you can get a sense, but there's some... When you look at a number sequence, I don't know...

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Like a Fibonacci number sequence, if you look at the first few numbers, that sequence could be completed in a lot of different ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And some are, if you think deeply, are more correct than others. There's a kind of intuitive simplicity and elegance to the correct solution.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes. I am personally not a fan of ambiguity in test questions, actually.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But I think you can have difficulty without requiring ambiguity simply by making the test require a lot of extrapolation over the training examples.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But the beautiful question is difficult, but gives away everything when you give the training example.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Basically, yes. Meaning that... So the tests I'm interested in creating are not necessarily difficult for humans, because human intelligence is the benchmark.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: They're supposed to be difficult for machines in ways that are easy for humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think an ideal test of human and machine intelligence is a test that is actionable, that highlights the need for progress and that highlights the direction in which you should be making progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think we'll talk about the RARC challenge and the test you've constructed, and you have these elegant examples.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think that highlight, like, this is really easy for us humans, but it's really hard for machines.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But on the designing an IQ test for IQs of higher than 160 and so on, you have to take that and put it on a stairway.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You have to think what is hard for humans. And that's a fascinating exercise in itself, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And it was an interesting question of what it takes to create a really hard question for humans, because you again have to do the same process as you mentioned, which is, you know, something basically where the experience that you have likely to have encountered throughout your whole life,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: even if you've prepared for IQ tests, which is a big challenge, that this will still be novel for you.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah, I mean, novelty is a requirement. You should not be able to practice for the questions that you're going to be tested on.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That's important, because otherwise what you're doing is not exhibiting intelligence. What you're doing is just retrieving what you've been exposed before.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's the same thing as deep learning model. If you train a deep learning model on all the possible answers, then it will ace your test in the same way that, you know, a stupid student can still ace the test if they cram for it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: They memorize, you know, a hundred different possible mock exams, and then they hope that the actual exam will be a very simple interpolation of the mock exams.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that student could just be a deep learning model at that point. But you can actually do that without any understanding of the material.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And in fact, many students pass the exams in exactly this way. And if you want to avoid that, you need an exam that's unlike anything they've seen that really probes their understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So how do we design an IQ test for machines, an intelligent test for machines?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: All right. So in the paper, I outline a number of requirements that you should expect of such a test.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And in particular, we should start by acknowledging the priors that we expect to be required in order to perform the test.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So we should be explicit about the priors, right? And if the goal is to compare machine intelligence and human intelligence, then we should assume human cognitive priors, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And secondly, we should make sure that we are testing for skill acquisition ability, skill acquisition efficiency in particular, and not for skill itself, meaning that every task featured in your test should be novel and should not be something that you can anticipate.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So for instance, it should not be possible to brute force the space of possible questions, right? To pre-generate every possible question and answer.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So it should be tasks that cannot be anticipated, not just by the system itself, but by the creators of the system, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah. You know what's fascinating? I mean, one of my favorite aspects of the paper and the work you do with the ARC challenge is the process of making priors explicit.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Just even that act alone is a really powerful one of like, what are... it's a really powerful question to ask of us humans. What are the priors that we bring to the table?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So the next step is like, once you have those priors, how do you use them to solve a novel task? But like, just even making the priors explicit is a really difficult and really powerful step.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that's like visually beautiful and conceptually, philosophically beautiful part of the work you did with, I guess, continue to do probably with the paper and the ARC challenge.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Can you talk about some of the priors that we're talking about here?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes. So a researcher has done a lot of work on what exactly are the knowledge priors that are innate to humans is Elizabeth Spelke from Harvard.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So she developed the core knowledge theory, which outlines four different core knowledge systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So systems of knowledge that we are basically either born with or that we are hardwired to acquire very early on in our development.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And there's no strong distinction between the two.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Like if you are primed to acquire a certain type of knowledge in just a few weeks, you might as well just be born with it. It's just part of who you are.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And so there are four different core knowledge systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Like the first one is the notion of objectness and basic physics. Like you recognize that something that moves currently, for instance, is an object.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So we intuitively, naturally, innately divide the world into objects based on this notion of physical coherence.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And in terms of filamentary physics, there's the fact that objects can bump against each other and the fact that they can occlude each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So these are things that we are essentially born with or at least that we are going to be acquiring extremely early because we're really hardwired to acquire them.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So a bunch of points, pixels that move together on objects are partly the same object.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes. I mean, I mean that like I don't smoke weed, but if I did, that's something I could sit like all night and just like think about.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I remember writing in your paper just objectness. I wasn't self-aware, I guess, of how that particular prior that that's such a fascinating prior that like that's the most basic one.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But objectness, just identity. Just objectness. It's very basic, I suppose, but it's so fundamental.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It is fundamental to human cognition.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah. And the second prior that's also fundamental is agentness, which is not a real world, a real world, but so agentness.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: The fact that some of these objects that you segment your environment into, some of these objects are agents. So what's an agent?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's basically it's an object that has goals.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That has what?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That has goals. There's a whole lot of pursuing goals. So for instance, if you see two dots moving in a roughly synchronized fashion, you will intuitively infer that one of the dots is pursuing the other.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So that one of the dots is and one of the dots is an agent and its goal is to avoid the other dot and one of the dots, the other dot is also an agent and its goal is to catch the first dot.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Pellky has shown that babies, as young as three months, identify agentness and goal directedness in their environment.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Another prior is basic geometry and topology, like the notion of distance, the ability to navigate in your environment and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: This is something that is fundamentally hardwired into our brain. It's in fact backed by very specific neural mechanisms, like for instance, grid cells and plate cells.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So it's something that's literally hard coded at the neural level in our hippocampus.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And the last prior would be the notion of numbers, like numbers are not actually a cultural construct. We are intuitively, innately able to do some basic counting and to compare quantities.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So it doesn't mean we can do arbitrary arithmetic.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Counting, the act of counting.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Counting like counting one, two, three, then maybe more than three. You can also compare quantities. If I give you three dots and five dots, you can tell the side with five dots as more dots.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So this is actually an innate prior.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So that said, the list may not be exhaustive. So Spelki is still pursuing the potential existence of new knowledge systems, for instance, knowledge systems that would deal with social relationships.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah, I mean, and that could be-

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Which is much less relevant to something like ARC or IQ test and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: There could be stuff that's like you said, rotation, symmetry, is really interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's very likely that there is, speaking about rotation, that there is in the brain a hard coded system that is capable of performing rotations.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: One famous experiment that people did in the, I don't remember who it was exactly, but in the 70s was that people found that if you asked people, if you give them two different shapes, and one of the shapes is a rotated version of the first shape, and you ask them,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: is that shape a rotated version of the first shape or not? What you see is that the time it takes people to answer is linearly proportional to the angle of rotation.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So it's almost like you have it somewhere in your brain, like a turntable with a fixed speed.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And if you want to know if two objects are rotated versions of each other, you put the object on the turntable, you let it move around a little bit, and then you stop when you have a match.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that's really interesting.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So what's the ARC challenge?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So in the paper I outlined all these principles that a good test of machine intelligence and human intelligence should follow, and the ARC challenge is one attempt to embody as many of these principles as possible.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So I don't think it's anywhere near a perfect attempt.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It does not actually follow every principle, but it is what I was able to do given the constraints.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So the format of ARC is very similar to classic IQ tests, in particular Raven's Progressive Metrices.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Raven's?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah, Raven's Progressive Metrices. I mean, if you've done IQ tests in the past, you know what it is probably, or at least you've seen it, even if you don't know what it's called.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And so you have a set of tasks, that's what they're called, and for each task you have training data, which is a set of input and output pairs.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So an input or output pair is a grid of colors, basically. The size of the grid is variable.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And you're given an input and you must transform it into the proper output.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And so you're shown a few demonstrations of a task in the form of existing input-output pairs, and then you're given a new input.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And you must provide, you must produce the correct output.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And the assumptions in ARC is that every task should only require core knowledge priors, should not require any outside knowledge.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: For instance, no language, no English, nothing like this.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: No concepts taken from all human experience, like trees, dogs, cats, and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So only tasks that are, reasoning tasks that are built on top of core knowledge priors.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And some of the tasks are actually explicitly trying to probe specific forms of abstraction.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Part of the reason why I wanted to create ARC is I'm a big believer in when you're faced with a problem as murky as understanding how to autonomously generate abstraction in a machine, you have to co-evolve the solution and the problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And so part of the reason why I designed ARC was to clarify my ideas about the nature of abstraction.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And some of the tasks are actually designed to probe bits of that theory.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And there are things that turn out to be very easy for humans to perform, including young kids, but turn out to be near impossible for machines.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So what have you learned from the nature of abstraction from designing that?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Can you clarify what you mean?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: One of the things you wanted to try to understand was this idea of abstraction.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes. So clarifying my own ideas about abstraction by forcing myself to produce tasks that would require the ability to produce that form of abstraction in order to solve them.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Got it. Okay. So, and by the way, just to, I mean, people should check out, I'll probably overlay if you're watching the video part, but the grid input output with the different colors on the grid.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That's it. That's, I mean, it's a very simple world, but it's kind of beautiful.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's very similar to classic IQ tests. Like it's not very original in that sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: The main difference with IQ tests is that we make the priors explicit, which is not usually the case in IQ tests.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So you might get explicit that everything should only be built on top of core knowledge priors.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I also think it's generally more diverse than IQ tests in general.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And it's, it perhaps requires a bit more manual work to produce solutions because you have to click around on a grid for a while.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Sometimes the grades can be as large as study by study cells.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So how did you come up? If you can reveal with the questions, like what's the process of the questions? Was it mostly you?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes. I came up with the questions. What, how difficult is it to come up with a question?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Like is this scalable to a much larger number?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: If you think, you know, with IQ tests, you might not necessarily want it to or need it to be scalable.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: With machines, it's possible you could argue that it needs to be scalable.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So there are a thousand questions, thousand tasks in total.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes. Including the test set, the prior test set.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think it's fairly difficult in the sense that a big requirement is that every task should be novel and unique and unpredictable.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Right. Like you don't want to create your own little world that is simple enough that it would be possible for a human to reverse and generate

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: and write down an algorithm that could generate every possible task and their solutions. So that would completely invalidate the test.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So you're constantly coming up with new stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah. You need a source of novelty, of unfakable novelty.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And one thing I found is that as a human, you are not a very good source of unfakable novelty.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And so you have to pace the creation of these tasks quite a bit.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: There are only so many unique tasks that you can do in a given day.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So that means coming up with truly original new ideas. Did psychedelics help you at all?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: No, I'm just kidding. But I mean, that's fascinating to think about.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So you would be like walking or something like that. Are you constantly thinking of something totally new?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: This is hard. This is hard.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I mean, I'm not saying you've done anywhere near a perfect job at it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: There is some amount of redundancy and there are many imperfections in ARC.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So that said, you should consider ARC as a work in progress. It is not the definitive state.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: The ARC tasks today are not definitive states of the test.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I want to keep refining it in the future.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I also think it should be possible to open up the creation of tasks to a broad audience to do crowdsourcing.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That would involve several levels of filtering, obviously.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But I think it's possible to apply crowdsourcing to develop a much bigger and much more diverse ARC data set.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That would also be free of potentially some of my own personal biases.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Does there always need to be a part of ARC that the test is hidden?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes, absolutely. It is impressive that the tests that you're using to actually benchmark algorithms

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: is not accessible to the people developing these algorithms.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Because otherwise, what's going to happen is that the human engineers are just going to solve the tasks themselves

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: and encode their solution in program form.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But that, again, what you're seeing here is the process of intelligence happening in the mind of the human.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And then you're just capturing its crystallized output.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But that crystallized output is not the same thing as the process that's generated.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's not intelligent in itself.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: By the way, the idea of crowdsourcing it is fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think the creation of questions is really exciting for people.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think there's a lot of really brilliant people out there that love to create these kinds of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: One thing that kind of surprised me that I wasn't expecting is that lots of people seem to actually enjoy ARC as a kind of game.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And I was really seeing it as a test, as a benchmark of fluid general intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And lots of people, including kids, are just starting to enjoy it as a game.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So I think that's encouraging.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah, I'm fascinated by it. There's a world of people who create IQ questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think that's a cool activity for machines and for humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Humans are themselves fascinated by taking the questions, like measuring their own intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I mean, that's just really compelling. It's really interesting to me, too.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: One of the cool things about ARC, you said, is it's kind of inspired by IQ tests or whatever.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It follows a similar process.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But because of its nature, because of the context in which it lives,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: it immediately forces you to think about the nature of intelligence as opposed to just the test of your own.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It forces you to really think.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I don't know if it's within the question, inherent in the question,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: or just the fact that it lives in a test that's supposed to be a test of machine intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Absolutely. As you solve ARC tasks as a human, you will be forced to basically introspect how you come up with solutions.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that forces you to reflect on the human problem-solving process

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: and the way your own mind generates abstract representations of the problems it's exposed to.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think it's due to the fact that the set of core knowledge priors that ARC is built upon is so small.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's all a recombination of a very, very small set of assumptions.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: OK, so what's the future of ARC?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So you held ARC as a challenge, as part of a Kaggle competition.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Do you think this is something that continues for five years, ten years, just continues growing?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes, absolutely. So ARC itself will keep evolving.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So I've talked about crowdsourcing. I think that's a good avenue.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Another thing I'm studying is I'll be collaborating with folks from the psychology department at NYU to do human testing on ARC.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And I think there are lots of interesting questions you can start asking,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: especially as you start correlating machine solutions to ARC tasks and the human characteristics of solutions.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: For instance, you can try to see if there's a relationship between the human perceived difficulty of a task and the machine perceived difficulty.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes, and exactly some measure of machine perceived difficulty.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's a nice playground in which to explore this very difference. It's the same thing as we talked about with autonomous vehicles.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: The things that could be difficult for humans might be very different than the things that are difficult.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And formalizing or making explicit that difference in difficulty may teach us something fundamental about intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So one thing I think we did well with ARC is that it's proving to be a very actionable test in the sense that machine performance on ARC started at very much zero initially,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: while humans found actually the tasks very easy.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that alone was like a big red flashing light saying that something is going on and that we are missing something.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And at the same time, machine performance did not stay at zero for very long.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Actually, within two weeks of the Kaggle competition, we started having a non-zero number.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And now the state of the art is around 20% of the test set solved.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And so ARC is actually a challenge where our capabilities start at zero, which indicates the need for progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But it's also not an impossible challenge. It's not accessible.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You can start making progress basically right away.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: At the same time, we are still very far from having solved it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that's actually a very positive outcome of the competition is that the competition has proven that there was no obvious shortcut to solve these tasks.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah, so the test held up.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah, exactly. That was the primary reason to do the Kaggle competition is to check if some clever person was going to hack the benchmark.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That did not happen, right? Like people who are solving the tasks are essentially doing it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Well, in a way, they're actually exploring some flaws of ARC that we will need to address in the future, especially they're essentially anticipating what sort of tasks may be contained in the test set, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Right. Which is kind of, yeah, that's the kind of hacking. It's human hacking of the test.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes. That said, with the state of the art, it's like 20% we're still very, very far from human level, which is closer to 100%.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And I do believe that it will take a while until we reach human parity on ARC.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that by the time we have human parity, we will have AI systems that are probably pretty close to human level in terms of general fluid intelligence, which is, I mean, they're not going to be necessarily human-like.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: They're not necessarily. You would not necessarily recognize them as being an AGI.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But they would be capable of a degree of generalization that matches the generalization performed by human fluid intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Sure. I mean, this is a good point in terms of general fluid intelligence to mention. In your paper, you describe different kinds of generalizations.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Local, broad, extreme. And there's a kind of hierarchy that you form.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120
