body.input: In the context of machine learning, you say a system generalizes if it can make sense of an input it has not yet seen.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that's what I would call system-centric generalization.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's generalization with respect to novelty for the specific system you're considering.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So I think a good test of intelligence should actually deal with developer-aware generalization, which is slightly stronger than system-centric generalization.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So developer-aware generalization would be the ability to generalize to novelty or uncertainty that not only the system itself has not access to, but the developer of the system could not have access to either.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That's a fascinating meta definition. So like the system is basically the edge case thing we're talking about with autonomous vehicles.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Neither the developer nor the system know about the edge cases in my encounter.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So the system should be able to generalize the thing that nobody expected, neither the designer of the training data nor obviously the contents of the training data.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That's a fascinating definition.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So you can see degrees of generalization as a spectrum. And the lowest level is what machine learning is trying to do, is the assumption that any new situation is going to be sampled from a static distribution of possible situations, and that you already have a representative sample of that distribution.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That's your training data. And so in machine learning, you generalize to a new sample from a known distribution. And the ways in which your new sample will be new or different are ways that are already understood by the developers of the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So you are generalizing to known unknowns for one specific task.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That's what you would call robustness. You are robust to things like noise, small variations, and so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: For one, a fixed known distribution that you know through your training data.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And a higher degree would be flexibility in machine intelligence. So flexibility would be something like an L5 self-driving car, or maybe a robot that can pass the coffee cup test, which is the notion that you would be given a random kitchen somewhere in the country, and you would have to go make a cup of coffee in that kitchen.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So flexibility would be the ability to deal with unknown unknowns. So things that could not, dimensions of variability that could not have been possibly foreseen by the creators of the system within one specific task.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So generalizing to the long tail of situations in self-driving, for instance, would be flexibility. So you have robustness, flexibility, and finally, you would have extreme generalization, which is basically flexibility,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: but instead of just considering one specific domain like driving or domestic robotics, you're considering an open-ended range of possible domains.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So a robot would be capable of extreme generalization if, let's say, it's designed and trained for cooking, for instance.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And if I buy the robot, and if it's able to teach itself gardening in a couple of weeks, it would be capable of extreme generalization, for instance.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So the ultimate goal is extreme generalization.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So creating a system that is so general that it could essentially achieve human skill parity over arbitrary tasks and arbitrary domains with the same level of improvisation and adaptation power as humans when it encounters new situations.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And it would do so over basically the same range of possible domains and tasks as humans and using essentially the same amount of training experience, of practice, as humans would require.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That would be human level extreme generalization.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So I don't actually think humans are anywhere near the optimal intelligence bound if there is such a thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So I think-

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: For humans or in general?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think it's quite likely that there is a hard limit to how intelligent any system can be.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But at the same time, I don't think humans are anywhere near that limit.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah, last time I think we talked, I think you had this idea that we're only as intelligent as the problems we face.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Sort of-

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes, intelligence-

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: We're upper bounded by the problems.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: In a way, yes, we are bounded by our environments and we are bounded by the problems we try to solve.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: What do you make of Neuralink and outsourcing some of the brain power, like brain-computer interfaces?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Do you think we can expand our, augment our intelligence?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I am fairly skeptical of neural interfaces because they are trying to fix one specific bottleneck in human-machine cognition,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: which is the bandwidth bottleneck input and output of information in the brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And my perception of the problem is that bandwidth is not at this time a bottleneck at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Meaning that we already have senses that enable us to take in far more information than what we can actually process.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Well, to push back on that a little bit, to sort of play devil's advocate a little bit, is if you look at the internet, the Wikipedia, let's say Wikipedia,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I would say that humans, after the advent of Wikipedia, are much more intelligent.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes, I think that's a good one. But that's also not about, that's about externalizing our intelligence via information processing systems,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: the external information processing systems, which is very different from brain-computer interfaces.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Right. But the question is whether if we have direct access, if our brain has direct access to Wikipedia without having...

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Your brain already has direct access to Wikipedia. It's on your phone. And you have your hands and your eyes and your ears and so on to access that information.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And the speed at which you can access it...

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Is bottlenecked by the cognition.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think it's already close, fairly close to optimal, which is why speed reading, for instance, does not work.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: The faster you read, the less you understand.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But maybe it's because it uses the eyes. So maybe...

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So I don't believe so. I think the brain is very slow.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It typically operates the fastest things that happen in the brain at the level of 50 milliseconds.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Forming a conscious thought can potentially take entire seconds.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Right. And you can already read pretty fast.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So I think the speed at which you can take information in and even the speed at which you can add with information can only be very incrementally improved.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think that if you're a very fast typer, if you're a very trained typer, the speed at which you can express your thoughts is already the speed at which you can form your thoughts.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Right. So that's kind of an idea that there are fundamental bottlenecks to the human mind.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But it's possible that everything we have in the human mind is just to be able to survive in the environment.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And there's a lot more to expand. Maybe, you know, you said the speed of the thought.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So I think augmenting human intelligence is a very valid and very powerful avenue.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that's what computers are about.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: In fact, that's what all of culture and civilization is about.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Culture is externalized cognition, and we rely on culture to think constantly.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah. I mean, that's another way.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Not just computers, not just phones and the internet.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I mean, all of culture, like language, for instance, is a form of externalized cognition.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Books are obviously externalized cognition.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And you can scale that externalized cognition far beyond the capability of the human brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And you could see civilization itself has capabilities that are far beyond any individual brain.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And we'll keep scaling it because it's not rebounded by individual brains.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's a different kind of system.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah. And that system includes non-humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: First of all, it includes all the other biological systems,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: which are probably contributing to the overall intelligence of the organism.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And then computers are part of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Non-human systems probably not contributing much, but AIs are definitely contributing to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Like Google Search, for instance, is a big part of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah. Yeah. A huge part. A part that we can't probably introspect.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Like how the world has changed in the past 20 years.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's probably very difficult for us to be able to understand until, of course, whoever created the simulation wherein is probably doing metrics measuring the progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: There was probably a big spike in performance. They're enjoying this.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So what are your thoughts on the Turing test and the Lobner Prize,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: which is one of the most famous attempts at the test of artificial intelligence by doing a natural language open dialogue test that's judged by humans as far as how well the machine did?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So I'm not a fan of the Turing test itself or any of its variants for two reasons.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So first of all, it's really copping out of trying to define and measure intelligence because it's entirely outsourcing that to a panel of human judges.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And these human judges, they may not themselves have any proper methodology.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: They may not themselves have any proper definition of intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: They may not be reliable. So the Turing test is already failing one of the core psychometric principles, which is reliability because you have biased human judges.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's also violating the standardization requirement and the freedom from bias requirement.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And so it's really a cop out because you are outsourcing everything that matters,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: which is precisely describing intelligence and finding a standalone test to measure it. You're outsourcing everything to people.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So it's really a cop out. And by the way, we should keep in mind that when Turing proposed the imitation game,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: it was not meaning for the imitation game to be an actual goal for the field of AI, an actual test of intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It was using the imitation game as a thought experiment in a philosophical discussion in his 1950 paper.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: He was trying to argue that theoretically it should be possible for something very much like the human mind, indistinguishable from the human mind, to be encoded in a Turing machine.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And at the time, that was a very daring idea. It was stretching credulity.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But nowadays, I think it's fairly well accepted that the mind is an information processing system and that you could probably encode it into a computer.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So another reason why I'm not a fan of this type of test is that the incentives that it creates are incentives that are not conducive to proper scientific research.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: If your goal is to trick, to convince a panel of human judges that they're talking to a human, then you have an incentive to rely on tricks and prestidigitation.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: In the same way that, let's say, you're doing physics and you want to solve teleportation.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And what if the test that you set out to pass is you need to convince a panel of judges that teleportation took place and they're just sitting there and watching what you're doing?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that is something that you can achieve with, you know, David Copperfield could achieve it in his show at Vegas, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But what he's doing is very elaborate, but it's not actually physics. It's not making any progress in our understanding of the universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: To push back on that, it's possible. That's the hope with these kinds of subjective evaluations, is that it's easier to solve it generally than it is to come up with tricks that convince a large number of judges.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: In practice, it turns out that it's very easy to deceive people in the same way that you can do magic in Vegas.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You can actually very easily convince people that they're talking to human when they're actually talking to an algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I disagree with that. I think it's easy. I would push, but it's not easy. It's doable.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's very easy because-

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I wouldn't say it's very easy though.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: We are biased. We have theory of mind. We are constantly projecting emotions, intentions, agentness. Agentness is one of our core innate priors, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: We are projecting these things on everything around us. If you paint a smiley on a rock, the rock becomes happy, you know, eyes.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And because we have this extreme bias that permits everything we see around us, it's actually pretty easy to trick people.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I totally disagree with that. You brilliantly put the anthropomorphization that we naturally do, the agentness of that word. Is that a real word?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: No, it's not a real word. I like it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But it's a good word. It's a useful word.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's a useful word. Let's make it real. It's a huge help, but I still think it's really difficult to convince.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: If you do like the Alexa Prize formulation where, you know, you talk for an hour, like there's formulations of the test you can create where it's very difficult.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So I like the Alexa Prize better because it's more pragmatic. It's more practical.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's actually incentivizing developers to create something that's useful as a human machine interface.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So that's slightly better than just the imitation.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So I like it. Your ideas like a test would hopefully help us in creating intelligent systems as a result.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Like if you create a system that passes it, it'll be useful for creating further intelligent systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes, at least.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah. I mean, I'm just to kind of comment. I'm a little bit surprised how little inspiration people draw from the Turing test today.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You know, the media and the popular press might write about it every once in a while.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: The philosophers might talk about it, but like most engineers are not really inspired by it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And I know I know you don't like the Turing test, but we'll have this argument another time.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: There's something inspiring about it, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: As a philosophical device, in a philosophical discussion, I think there's something very interesting about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I don't think it is, in practical terms, I don't think it's conducive to progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And one of the reasons why is that, you know, I think being very human-like, being indistinguishable from a human is actually the very last step in the creation of machine intelligence.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That the first AIs that will show strong generalization, that will actually implement human-like broad cognitive abilities, they will not actually behave or look anything like humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Human likeness is the very last step in that process.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And so a good test is a test that points you towards the first step on the ladder, not towards the top of the ladder, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So to push back on that, I usually agree with you on most things.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I remember you, I think, at some point tweeting something about the Turing test not being counterproductive or something like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And I think a lot of very smart people agree with that.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I, you know, computation speaking, not very smart person, disagree with that because I think there's some magic to the interactivity with other humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So to push, to play devil's advocate on your statement, it's possible that in order to demonstrate the generalization abilities of a system, you have to show your ability, in conversation, show your ability to adjust, adapt to the conversation through, not just like as a standalone system, but through the process of like the interaction, the game theoretic.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Where you're, you really are changing the environment by your actions.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So in the ARC challenge, for example, you're an observer.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You can't, you can't scare the test into, into changing.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You can't talk to the test.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You can't play with it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So there's some aspect of that interactivity that becomes highly subjective, but it feels like it could be conducive to generalizing.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I think you make a great point. The interactivity is very good setting to force a system to show adaptation, to show generalization.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That said, you're at the same time, it's not something very scalable because you rely on human judges. It's not something reliable because the human judges may not, may not be.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So you don't like human judges.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Basically, yes. And I think so. I love the idea of interactivity.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I initially wanted an ARC test that had some amount of interactivity where your score on a task would not be one or zero, if you can solve it or not, but would be the number of attempts that you can make before you hit the right solution.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Which means that now you can start applying the scientific method as you solve ARC tasks that you can start formulating hypothesis and probing the system to see whether the hypothesis, the observation will match the hypothesis or not.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It would be amazing if you could also, even higher level than that, measure the quality of your attempts, which of course is impossible.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But again, that gets subjective.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Like how good was your thinking? Like it's the...

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: How efficient was...

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So one thing that's interesting about this notion of scoring you as how many attempts you need is that you can start producing tasks that are way more ambiguous.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Because with the different attempts, you can actually probe that ambiguity.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So that's in a sense, which is how good can you adapt to the uncertainty and reduce the uncertainty?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes. It's half fast. It's the efficiency with which to reduce uncertainty in program space. Exactly.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Very difficult to come up with that kind of task though.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah. So I would love to be able to create something like this. In practice, it would be very, very difficult, but yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I mean, what you're doing, what you've done with the ARC challenge is brilliant. I'm also not, I'm surprised that it's not more popular, but I think it's picking up.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It has its niche. It has its niche.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah. What are your thoughts about another test that I talked with Marcus Hodder? He has the Hodder Prize for compression of human knowledge and the idea is really sort of quantify and reduce the test of intelligence purely to just the ability to compress.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: What's your thoughts about this intelligence as compression?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I mean, it's a very fun test because it's such a simple idea. Like you're given Wikipedia, basically English Wikipedia, and you must compress it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And so it stems from the idea that cognition is compression, that the brain is basically a compression algorithm.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: This is a very old idea. It's a very, I think, striking and beautiful idea. I used to believe it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I eventually had to realize that it was very much a flawed idea. So I no longer believe that cognition is compression.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But I can tell you what's the difference. So it's very easy to believe that cognition and compression are the same thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So Jeff Hockens, for instance, says that cognition is prediction. And of course, prediction is basically the same thing as compression.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's just including the temporal axis. And it's very easy to believe this because compression is something that we do all the time, very naturally.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: We are constantly compressing information. We have this bias towards simplicity. We're constantly trying to organize things in our mind and around us to be more regular.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So it's a beautiful idea. It's very easy to believe. There is a big difference between what we do with our brains and compression.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So compression is actually kind of a tool in the human cognitive toolkit that is used in many ways. But it's just a tool.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It is a tool for cognition. It is not cognition itself. And the big fundamental difference is that cognition is about being able to operate in future situations that include fundamental uncertainty and novelty.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So for instance, consider a child at age 10. And so they have 10 years of life experience. They've gotten pain, pleasure, rewards, and punishment in that period of time.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: If you were to generate the shortest behavioral program that would have basically run that child over these 10 years in an optimal way,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: the shortest optimal behavioral program given the experience of that child so far, well, that program, that compressed program, this is what you would get if the mind of the child was a compression algorithm essentially,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: would be utterly unable, inappropriate to process the next 70 years in the life of that child.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So in the models we build of the world, we are not trying to make them actually optimally compressed.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: We are using compression as a tool to promote simplicity and efficiency in our models.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But they are not perfectly compressed because they need to include things that are seemingly useless today, that have seemingly been useless so far,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: but that may turn out to be useful in the future because you just don't know the future.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that's the fundamental principle that cognition, that intelligence arises from is that you need to be able to run appropriate behavioral programs,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: except you have absolutely no idea what sort of context, environment, and situation they're going to be running in.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And you have to deal with that uncertainty, with that future novelty.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So an analogy that you can make is with investing, for instance.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: If I look at the past 20 years of stock market data and I use a compression algorithm to figure out the best trading strategy,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: it's going to be, you know, you buy Apple stock, then maybe the past few years you buy Tesla stock or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But is that strategy still going to be true for the next 20 years?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Well, actually, probably not.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Which is why if you're a smart investor, you're not just going to be following the strategy that corresponds to compression of the past.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You're going to have a balanced portfolio, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Because you just don't know what's going to happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Totally new things. I mean, I guess in that same sense, the compression is analogous to what you talked about, which is like local or robust generalization versus extreme generalization.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's much closer to that side of being able to generalize in the local sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That's why, you know, as humans, when we are children, in our education, so a lot of it is driven by place, driven by curiosity.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: We are not efficiently compressing things. We're actually exploring.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: We are retaining all kinds of things from our environment that seem to be completely useless because they might turn out to be eventually useful, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that's what cognition is really about. And what makes it antagonistic to compression is that it is about hedging for future uncertainty.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Officially. Officially hedging.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Cognition leverages compression as a tool to promote efficiency, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: In that sense, it's like Einstein said, make it simpler, but not too simple.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So you want to, compression simplifies things, but you don't want to make it too simple.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes. So a good model of the world is going to include all kinds of things that are completely useless, actually, just in case.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Because you need diversity in the same way that in your portfolio, you need all kinds of stocks that may not have performed well so far, but you need diversity.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And the reason you need diversity is because fundamentally you don't know what you're doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And the same is true of the human mind is that it needs to behave appropriately in the future and it has no idea what the future is going to be like.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's not going to be like the past. So compressing the past is not appropriate because the past is not predictive of the future.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yeah. History repeats itself, but not perfectly.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I don't think I asked you last time the most inappropriately absurd question.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: We've talked a lot about intelligence, but the bigger question from intelligence is of meaning.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Intelligence systems are kind of goal oriented. They're always optimizing for goal.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: If you look at the Hunter Prize, actually, there's always a clean formulation of a goal.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But the natural question for us humans, since we don't know our objective function, is what is the meaning of it all?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So the absurd question is what Francois Chollet do you think is the meaning of life?

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: What's the meaning of life? Yeah, that's a big question.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And I think I can give you my answer, at least one of my answers.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So you know, one thing that's very important in understanding who we are is that everything that makes up ourselves, that makes up who we are, even your most personal thoughts, is not actually your own.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Even your most personal thoughts are expressed in words that you did not invent and are built on concepts and images that you did not invent.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: We are very much cultural beings. We are made of culture. What makes us different from animals, for instance.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So everything about ourselves is an echo of the past, an echo of people who lived before us. That's who we are.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And in the same way, if we manage to contribute something to the collective edifice of culture,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: a new idea, maybe a beautiful piece of music, a work of art, a grand theory, a new words maybe,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: that something is going to become a part of the minds of future humans essentially forever.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So everything we do creates ripples that propagate into the future.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that's in a way, this is our path to immortality, is that as we contribute things to culture, culture in turn becomes future humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And we keep influencing people thousands of years from now.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So our actions today create ripples. And these ripples, I think, basically sum up the meaning of life.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: In the same way that we are the sum of the interactions between many different ripples that came from our past,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: we are ourselves creating ripples that will propagate into the future.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And that's why this seems like perhaps an naive thing to say, but we should be kind to others during our time on Earth,

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: because every act of kindness creates ripples. And in reverse, every act of violence also creates ripples.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And you want to carefully choose which kind of ripples you want to create, and you want to propagate into the future.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And in your case, first of all, beautifully put, but in your case, creating ripples into the future human and future AGI systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Yes. It's fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: All six of us.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: I don't think there's a better way to end it, Francois, as always for a second time, and I'm sure many times in the future, it's been a huge honor.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: You're one of the most brilliant people in the machine learning, computer science, science world.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Again, it's a huge honor. Thanks for talking today.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: It's been a pleasure. Thanks a lot for having me. We appreciate it.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: And now let me leave you with some words from René Descartes in 1668, an excerpt of which Francois includes in his On the Measure of Intelligence paper.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: If there were machines which bore a resemblance to our bodies and imitated our actions as closely as possible for all practical purposes, we should still have two very certain means of recognizing that they were not real men.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: The first is that they could never use words or put together signs, as we do in order to declare our thoughts to others.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: For we can certainly conceive of a machine so constructed that it utters words and even utters words that correspond to bodily actions causing a change in its organs.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: But it is not conceivable that such a machine should produce different arrangements of words so as to give an appropriately meaningful answer to whatever is said in its presence as the dullest of men can do.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Here Descartes is anticipating the Turing test, and the argument still continues to this day.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Secondly, he continues, even though some machines might do some things as well as we do them, or perhaps even better, they would inevitably fail in others, which would reveal that they're acting not from understanding, but only from the disposition of their organs.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: This is an incredible quote. Whereas reason is a universal instrument which can be used in all kinds of situations, these organs need some particular action.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: Hence, it is for all practical purposes impossible for a machine to have enough different organs to make it act in all the contingencies of life in the way in which our reason makes us act.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: That's the debate between mimicry memorization versus understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: François Chollet: Measures of Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #120

body.input: So, thank you for listening and hope to see you next time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: To support it, please check out our sponsors in the description.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And now, here's my conversation with Yaron Brook and Yoram Hozoni.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I attended the excellent debate between the two of you yesterday at UT Austin.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The debate was between ideas of conservatism, represented by Yoram Hozoni,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and ideas of individualism, represented by Yaron Brook.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Let's start with the topics of the debate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Yoram, how do you define conservatism, maybe in the way you were thinking about it yesterday?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: What do you are some principles of conservatism?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Let me define it, and then we can get into principles, if you want.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: When I talk about political conservatism, I'm talking about a political standpoint that

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: regards the recovery, elaboration, and restoration of tradition

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: as the key to maintaining a nation and strengthening it through time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: This is something that if you have time to talk about it, like we do on the show,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: it's worth emphasizing that conservatism is not like liberalism or Marxism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Liberalism and Marxism are both kind of universal theories.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: They claim to be able to tell you what's good for human beings at all times, in all places.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Conservatism is a little bit different because it's going to carry different values

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: in every nation, in every tribe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Even every family, you can say, has somewhat different values.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: These loyalty groups, they compete with one another.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That's the way human beings work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So it's deeply rooted in history of that particular area of land.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Well, I wouldn't necessarily say land.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You're right that many forms of conservatism are tied to a particular place.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So how does the implementation of conservatism to you differ from the ideal of conservatism,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: the implementations you've seen of political conservatism in the United States and the rest of the world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Just to give some context, because it's a loaded term, like most political terms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So when people think about conservative in the United States, they think about the Republican Party.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Can you kind of disambiguate some of this?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: What are we supposed to think about?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Yeah, that's a really important question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Usually the word conservative is associated with Edmund Burke and with the English common law tradition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Going back centuries and centuries, there's kind of a classical English conservative tradition

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: that goes Fortescue, Hooker, Koch, Seldon, Hale, Burke, Blackstone before Burke.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: If you take that kind of as a benchmark and you compare it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: then you can compare it to things like the American Federalist Party at the time of the American founding

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: is in many respects very much in keeping with that tradition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: As you go forward, there's an increasing mix of liberalism into conservatism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I think by the time you get to the 1960s with William Buckley and Frank Meyer,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: the jargon term is fusionism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: By the time you get there, it's arguable that their conservatism isn't very conservative anymore,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: that it's kind of a public liberalism mixed with a private conservatism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: A lot of the debate that we have today about what does the word conservatism actually mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: a lot of the confusion comes from that, comes from the fact that on the one hand,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: we have people who use the term, I think, properly historically to refer to this common law tradition

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: of which Burke was a spokesman.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But there are lots of other people who when they say conservative, they just mean liberal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I think that's a big problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I mean, it's a problem just to have an intelligent debate is difficult when people are using the word almost too antithetical.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: What would you say the essential idea of conservatism is? Time?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You mentioned your father's a physicist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So a lot of physicists, when they form models of the universe, they don't consider time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So everything is dealt with instantaneously.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: A particle is represented fully by its current state, velocity and position.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You're saying, so you're arguing with all of physics and your father, as we always do,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: that their time matters in conservatism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That's the fundamental element is the full history matters.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And you cannot separate the individual from the history, from the roots that they come from.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The parallel in political theory is what's called rationalism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I guess we'll probably talk about that some.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Rationalism is kind of an instantaneous, timeless thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Before I mentioned that liberalism and various Enlightenment theories, they don't include time at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Their goal is to say, look, there's such a thing as universal human reason.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: All human beings, if they reason properly, will come to the same conclusions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: If that's true, then it removes the time consideration.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It removes tradition and context.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Because everywhere where you are at any time, you ought to be able to use reason

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and come to the same conclusions about politics or morals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So that's a theory like Immanuel Kant or John Locke is an example.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Hobbes is an example.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That kind of political theorizing really does say at a given instant,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: we can know pretty much everything that we need to know, at least the big things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And conservatism is the opposite.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's a traditionalist view, exactly as you say, that says that history is crucial.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So, Yaron, you say that history is interesting, but perhaps not crucial.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: If in the context of individualism.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I think there's a false dichotomy he presented here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And that is that one view holds that you can derive anything from a particular historical path

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and kind of an empirical view.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And if we know the history, we know where we should be tomorrow.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: We know where we should stand today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And the other path is we ignore history, we ignore facts, we ignore what's going on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: We can derive from some a priori axioms, we can derive a truth right now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And both are false. Both of those views in my view are false.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And, you know, Ayn Rand and I reject both of those views.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I think the better thinkers of the Enlightenment did as well,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: although they sometimes fall into the trap of appearing like rationalists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And, Yom and I agree on one thing, and that is that Kant is one of...

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You know, we've talked about this in the past, Lex.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But we both hate Kant. We both think Kant is...

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I at least think Kant is probably the most destructive philosopher since Plato,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: who was pretty destructive himself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And part of the problem is that Kant divorces reason from reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That is, he divorces reason from history.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: He divorces reason from experience because we don't have direct experience of reality according to Kant, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: We're removed from that direct experience.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But I view Kant as the anti-Enlightenment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That is, I view Kant as the destroyer of good Enlightenment thinking and Yoram.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I acknowledge a lot of history of philosophy, people who do history of philosophy,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: view Kant as the embodiment of the Enlightenment, that is the ultimate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But I think that's a mistake.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I think both Rousseau and Kant are fundamentally the goal, the mission in life is to destroy the Enlightenment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So my view is neither of those options are the right option.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That is, the true reason-based...

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Reason is not divorced from reality. It's quite the opposite.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Reason is a tool. It's a faculty of identifying and integrating what.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's identifying and integrating the facts of reality as we know them through sense perception

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: or through the study of history, through what actually happened.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So it's the integration of those facts.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's the knowledge of that history.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And then what we do is we abstract away principles based on what's worked in the past,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: what hasn't worked in the past, the consequences of different ideas, different past, different actions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: We abstract away principles that then can be universal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Not always. We make mistakes, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: We can come up with a universal principle. It turns out that it's not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But if we have the whole scope of human history, we can derive principles as we do in life, as individuals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: We derive principles that are then truths that we can live by.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But you don't do that by ignoring history.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You do that by learning history, by understanding history, by understanding, in a sense, tradition and where it leads to,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and then trying to do better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I think good thinkers are constantly trying to do better based on what they know about the past and what they know about the present.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: What's the difference between studying history on a journey of reason and tradition?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So you mentioned that Burke understood that reason begins with inherited tradition yesterday.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So what's the difference between studying history, but then being free to go any way you want,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and tradition where it feels more, I don't want to say a negative term like burden,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: but there's more of a momentum that forces you to go the same way as your ancestors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's the recognition that people are wrong, often are wrong.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And parents?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Including your parents, including your teachers, including everybody.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Everybody is potentially wrong and that you can't accept anybody just because they happen to come before you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That is, you have to evaluate and judge, and you have to have a standard by which to evaluate and judge the actions of those who came before you,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256
