body.input: I mean, Jefferson and Adams for decades didn't even speak to each other, though they did make up and had a fascinating relationship.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You and I are making up too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's like the founding fathers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You know, there's massive debate and discussion, but I don't agree with the characterization of pain and Jefferson.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I don't think it's just to call them rationalists because I don't think they're rationalists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: People who've looked at history, at the problems in history, and remember, this is the 18th century,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and they were coming out of 100 years earliest on the bloodiest wars in all of human history,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: were happening in Europe, many of them over religion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You know, they'd seen what was going on in France and other countries where people were starving

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and where kings were frolicking in palaces in spite of that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: They were very aware of the relative freedom that the British tradition had given Englishmen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I think they knew that, they understood that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I think they were building on that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: They were taking the observation of the past and trying to come up with a more perfect system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I think they did.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And in that sense, I'm a huge fan of Jefferson.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You know, there are two things that I think are unfortunate about Jefferson.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: One is that he continued to hold slaves, which is very unfortunate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And the second is early support for the French Revolution, which I think is a massive mistake.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I would be surprised if he regretted it later in life, given the consequences.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But, you know, they were trying to derive principles by which they could establish a new state.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And yes, there was some, there was pushback by some and there was disagreements.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And the Constitution in the end is, to some extent, a form of compromise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's still one of the great documents of all of human history, political documents, the Constitution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Although I think it's inferior to the Declaration.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I'm a huge fan of the Declaration.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I think one of the mistakes the conservatives makes, one of the mistakes the Supreme Court makes and American judiciary makes is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: assuming the two documents are separate, I think Lincoln is actually right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You can't understand the Constitution without understanding the Declaration,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: the Declaration of what set the context and what sets everything up for the Constitution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Individual rights are the key concept there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And one of the challenges was that some of the compromises,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and compromise is not necessarily between groups, but compromises that even Jefferson made and others made regarding individual rights,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: set America on a path that we're suffering from today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I mentioned three last night.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: One was slavery.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Obviously, that was a horrific compromise, one that American not just paid for with a civil war,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: when over 1000 young men died because of it, but the suffering of black slaves for all those years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But then the whole issue of racial tensions in this country for a century, and to this day, really, is a consequence of that initial compromise.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Who knows what the counterfactual is in America if there's a civil war right at the founding, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Because there would have been a war no matter what.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But if it had happened in the late 18th century, early 19th century, rather than waiting until 1860s.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But then second was Jefferson's embrace of public education, his founding of the University of Virginia,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: which I think is a great tragedy, which nobody agrees with me on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So that's one of the areas where I'm pretty radical.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And then they embrace, both by Jefferson and by Hamilton, for different reasons, but an embrace by both of them, of government role in the economy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I do finance, so I know a little bit about finance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And the debate between Jefferson and Hamilton about banking is fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But at the end of the day, both wanted a role for government in banking.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: They both didn't trust.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Jefferson didn't trust big financial interests.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Hamilton wanted to capture some of those financial interests for the state.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And as a consequence, we set America on a path where, in my view, regulation always leads to more regulation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: There's never a case where regulation decreases.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And we started out with a certain regulatory body around banks and a recognition that it was okay to regulate the economy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So once we get into the late 19th century, it's fine to regulate the railroads.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's fine to pass antitrust laws.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's fine to then continue on the path of where we are today, which is heavy, heavy, heavy, massive involvement of government in every aspect of our country.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: In every aspect of our economy and really in every aspect of our life because of education.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So I think the country was founded on certain mistakes, and we haven't been willing to question those mistakes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And in a sense, we've only moved in the opposite direction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And now America has become – whereas I think it was founded on the idea of the primacy of the individual, the sanctity of the individual,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: at least as an idea, even if not fully implemented, I think now that's completely lost.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I don't think anybody really is an advocate out there for individualism in politics or for true freedom in politics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: We'll get to individualism, but let me ask the Beatles and the Rolling Stones question about the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Because it's like which document – Beatles, which document is more important?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's obvious to the Beatles, right? Is there even a question?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Is there even a question? But let me then even zoom in further and ask you to pick your favorite song.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So what ideas in the Constitution or the Declaration of Independence do you think are the most important to the success of the United States of America?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I'll answer the question, but before answering the question, I want to descent from – register a descent from your own –

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Is it the public education? Is it which –

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: No, no, no. Actually, we're not so – look, we're not so far apart on public education.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I'm actually kind of surprised that you're so anti-Bismarck because his public school system – his national public school system was created in order to stick it to the church.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It was the church that ran the schools before then.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Okay, so that's a different –

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I'm all for sticking it to the church.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Any opportunity, but not – not when the alternative is the nation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I'd rather see – I'd rather see free educational system, you know, where freedom is in education.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Okay, so I want to register a descent about Lincoln. Look, Lincoln is an important figure and a great man, and he was presiding over a country, which at that point was pretty Jeffersonian in terms of its self-perception.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: He said what he needed to say. I'm not going to criticize him.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But I don't accept the idea that the Declaration of Independence, which starts one revolution, is of a piece with the second constitution, the Constitution of 1787, the Nationalist Constitution, which is effectively a counterrevolution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: What happens is there is a revolution. It's based on certain principles. There are a lot – not exactly, but in many ways resembles the later ideas of the French Revolution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And what the Federalist Party does, the Nationalist Conservative Party does, is a counterrevolution to reinstate the old English Constitution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So these documents are – if you're willing to accept the evidence of history, they are in many respects contrary to one another.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And so if I'm asked what's the most important values that are handed down by these documents, I don't have an objection to life, liberty, and property, all of which are really important things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I do have an objection to the pompous overreach of these are self-evident, which is absurd.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: They can't be self-evident. If they were self-evident, then somebody would have come up with them like 2,000 years before. It's not self-evident.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And so that's damaging. I like the conservative preamble of the Constitution, which describes the purposes of the national government that's being established.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: There are seven purposes. A more perfect union, which is the principle of cohesion, justice, domestic peace, common defense, the general welfare, which is the welfare of the public as a thing that's not only individuals, but there is such a thing as a general welfare, liberty, which we agree is absolutely crucial, and posterity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The idea that the purpose of the government is to be able to sustain and grow this independent nation, and not only to guarantee rights no matter what happens.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But you don't like the, we hold these truths to be self-evident. So you definitely be those guy. You don't want the pompous. You don't need that revolutionary strength.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Look, I just, I think that that expression, self-evident truth, it does tremendous damage because it, instead of a moderate skepticism, which says, look, we may not know everything. It says, look, we know everything. Here it is. Here's what we know. We know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: We don't know everything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: No, we think.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So, you know, I'll agree with you, Oram. I don't like self-evident. I don't like self-evident because he's actually right. It's not self-evident. These are massive achievements.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: These are massive achievements of enlightened thinking, of studying history, of understanding human nature, of deriving a truth from 3,000 years of historical knowledge and a better understanding of human nature and a capacity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's using reason in some ways better than any human beings have. I mean, the founding fathers are giants historically, in my view, because they came up with these truths. I do think they're truths, but they're certainly not self-evident.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I mean, if they were, Oram is right. They would have discovered them thousands of years earlier or everybody would accept them, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I mean, how many people today think that those, what they state in the document is true? Pretty much, you know, five people. I don't know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I don't know. It's very-

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That's your criticism of modern society. Yes, we'll get there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's very, very few people recognize that if they were self-evident, bam, everybody would have become, you know, would have accepted the American Revolution as truth and that was it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: A lot of work has to go into understanding and describing and convincing people about those truths. But I completely disagree with you, Oram, about this idea or I'll voice my dissent, as we said.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Register your official dissent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: About A, this being two different revolutions and B, that the American Revolution was at any similarity to the French Revolution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You know that Jefferson and Payne were, they were in France running a different revolution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I know, but they were writing constantly. I mean, they were in communication with Madison. There was a lot of input going on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I know, and Jefferson's sitting there in Paris pulling his hair out because Madison has come under the influence of these nationalists and he can't believe it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The reality is that the difference between the French Revolution and the American Revolution is vast and it is a deep philosophical difference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And it's a difference that expressed, I think, between the differences. You know, Oram, in his writings, lumps Rousseau with Locke and with Voltaire and with others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I think that's wrong. I think Rousseau is very different than the others. I think, again, Rousseau is an anti-enlightenment figure. Rousseau is in many respects harkening back to a past, an ancient past.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I think a completely distorted view of human nature, of human mind. He rejects reason. I mean, Rousseau is on the premise that reason is the end of humanity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Reason is the destruction of humanity. Reason is how we get civilization. And civilization is awful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I don't disagree. We're only talking about different texts. When I say Rousseau, I'm just talking about the social contract.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Yeah, but the social contract, there's similarity between others, but he takes it in a completely different direction. And we agree social contract is a bad idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But they can have a contract that you don't actually voluntarily accept. But Rousseau is the French Revolution. Rousseau is about destruction and mayhem and chaos and anarchy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: He is the spirit behind the French Revolution. I think the American Revolution is a complete rejection of Rousseau. I think Jefferson is a complete rejection of Rousseau.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I don't think Jefferson is a fan of Rousseau. He is of Voltaire and he certainly is of Montesquieu.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: If you look at the Federalist papers, the intellectual most cited in the Federalist papers, I think in terms of just the number of times it's cited, is Montesquieu.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So I think that the American Revolution is an individualistic revolution. It is a revolution about the rights of the individual.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The French Revolution is a negation of the rights of the individual. It's a collectivistic revolution. It's not quite the Marxist revolution of the proletarian,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: but it's defining people in classes and it's a rebellion against a certain class and yeah, kill them all, right? Off with their heads.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It is a negation. It's about egalitarianism in the sense of equality of outcome, not in a sense of equality before the law or equality of rights, which is the Jeffersonian sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So I think it's wrong to lump Jefferson into the fraternity, egalitarian notion of the French, which is far more similar to what ultimately became socialism and Marxism and kind of that tradition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's anti-individualistic, the French Revolution is, whereas the American Revolution, the first one, is individualistic. It's all about individual rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And while there's certain phrases in the Declaration of Independence that I don't agree with, it's beautifully written and it's a magnificent document.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So it's hard for me to say I don't agree. Who am I? These were giants. Self-evident is one of them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I'm not particularly crazy about endowed by the creator, but I like the fact that it's creator and not God or not a specific creator, but just kind of a more general thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But putting those two ashes aside, it's the greatest political document in all of human history, in my view, by far.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Nothing comes close. It is a document that identifies the core principles of political truism, of truth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That is, the role of government is to preserve and to protect these rights, these inalienable rights, and that is so crucial that these rights are inalienable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That is, a majority can't vote them out. Revelation can't vote them out. This is what is required for human liberty and human freedom.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The right, that is, the sanction, the freedom to act on your own behalf, to act based on your own judgment, and as long as you're not interfering with other people's rights, you are free to do so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That is such a profound truth, and that to me is the essence of political philosophy. That's the beginning, and it's based on, just to not fall into, you're all I'm going to say it's a rationalist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's based on a whole history of what happens when you gate that. It's based on looking at England and seeing to the extent that they practiced a respect for individual liberty, a property of freedom, good things happened.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So let's take that all the way. Let's not compromise on that. Let's be consistent with the good and reject the bad.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And when England goes away, distances itself from the rights of man, from the idea of a right to property and so on, bad things happen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And when they go to, let's go all in, and I'm all in on the right to life, liberty, property, and the pursuit of happiness.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I think the idea of pursuit of happiness is profound because it's a moral statement. It's a statement that says that sanctions and says that ultimately people should be allowed to make their own judgments and live their lives as they see fit based on how they view happiness.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: They might be right, they might be wrong, but we're not going to dictate what happiness entails and dictate to people how they should live their lives. We're going to let them figure that out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So it has this self-interested moral code kind of embedded in it. So I think it's a beautiful statement.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So I think the declaration is key. And I think there was an experiment, and the experiment was post, in that period of before the Constitution, where the experiment was let's let the states, let's have a kind of a loose confederation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Let's have the states experiment with setting up their own constitutions and role of government, and we won't have any kind of unity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I think what they realized, and I think even Jefferson realized, is that that was not workable because many of the states were starting to significantly violate rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: There was nothing to unify, there was nothing to really protect the vision of the declaration.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You needed to establish a nation, which is what the Constitution does. It establishes a nation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But the purpose of that was to put everybody under one set of laws that protected rights. The focus was still on the protection of rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I agree with six of the seven of the principles.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Which did disagree with?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The common welfare, which the general welfare, which I worry about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I think in the way the founders understood it, I think I probably agreed with it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But it's such an ambiguous.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I'm sure you don't agree.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Maybe I don't.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Can you state the general welfare principle?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Well, the idea that part of the role of government is to secure the general welfare.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Look, this is something we didn't get to in the debate, we really should have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Is the question of whether there is such a thing as a common good or a public interest or a national interest or a general welfare.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Do these terms mean anything other than the good of all of the individuals in the country?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That's why I object to it because I think it's too easy to interpret it as.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So I interpret it as, well, what's good for a general, a group, a common people, a collection of individuals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So what's good for the individual is good for the common welfare.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But I understand that that's something that is hard for people to grasp and not the common understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So I would have skipped the general welfare in order to avoid the fact that now the general welfare includes the government telling you what gender you should be assigned.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So I would have wanted to have skipped that completely.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So I think the Constitution is pretty consistent with the Declaration with a few exceptions, the general welfare.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But perfection is a difficult thing to find, particularly for me politically.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But it's a magnificent document, the Constitution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It doesn't quite rise to the level, I think, of the Declaration, but it's a magnificent document.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Because, and this is the difference, I think, between the English Constitution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Here's what I see is the difference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The difference is that the Constitution is written in the context of why do we have a separation of powers, for example?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: We have a separation of powers in order to make sure that the government only does what the government is supposed to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And what is the government supposed to do?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Well, fundamentally, it's supposed to protect rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I mean, all of those seven, or at least six of the seven, are about protecting rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: They're about protecting us from foreign invaders.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: They're about protecting peace within the country.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: They're about preserving this protection of rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And why do we have the separation?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So that we make sure that no one of those entities, the executive or the legislature, judicial, can violate rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Because there's always somebody looking over their shoulder.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: There's always somebody who can veto their power.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But there's a purpose to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And that purpose is clearly signified and characterized.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And that's why I think the Bill of Rights was written in order to add to the clarification of what exactly we mean.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: What is the purpose?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The purpose is to preserve rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And that's why we need to elaborate what those rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And Madison's objection to the Bill of Rights was to say not that he objected to having protection of rights,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: but to listing them because he was worried that other rights that were not listed would not be.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And his worry was completely justified because it's exactly what's happened.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's like the only reason we have free speech in America is we've got it in writing as a First Amendment.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: If we didn't have it in writing, it would have been gone a long time ago.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And the reason we don't have, for example, the freedom to negotiate a contract, you know, independent government regulation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: is that was not listed as a right in the bill, even though I think it's clearly covered under the Constitution and certainly under the Declaration.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So there was a massive mistake done in the Bill of Rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: They tried to cover it with the Ninth Amendment, but it never really stuck.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: This idea that the non-enumerated rights that are still in place.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So I don't see this as a second revolution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I think it's a fix to a flaw that happened.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's a fix that allowed the expansion of the protection of rights to all states by creating a national entity to protect those rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And that's what ultimately led to slavery going away.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You know, under the initial agreement, slavery would have been there in perpetuity because states were sovereign in a way that under the new Constitution they were not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And in a sense, the Constitution sets in motion the Declaration and then the Constitution set in motion the Civil War.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The Civil War has to happen because at the end of the day, you cannot have some states with a massive violation of rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: What's more from violation of rights and slavery?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And some states that recognize it's not, it inevitably leads to the Civil War.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Jeroen was just saying that, you know, other than the general welfare, these principles are about individual liberties.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I think I just don't think you can read it that way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The first stated purpose of the Constitution of 1787 is in order to form a more perfect union.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: A more perfect union, it's describing a characteristic of the whole.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It is not a characteristic of any individual.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: If you look at how the individuals are doing, you don't know whether their union is more or less perfect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So what they're doing is they're looking at the condition in which in order to be able to fight the Battle of Yorktown, they have to, somebody has to write a personal check in order to be able to move armies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: A more perfect union is a more cohesive union.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It's the ability to get all of these different individuals to do one focused thing when it's necessary to do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Well, it's more than that, right? So I agree with that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But for what purpose?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That is, and this is why, you know, this is why it's so hard with these historical documents, because there's a context and there's a thinking that they can't write everything down, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Which is sad, because I wish they had.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: What's the purpose of a more perfect union?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The purpose of the more perfect union is to preserve the liberty of the individuals within that union.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: How do you know?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Because if you look, what's the rest? So what is the common defense?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The common defense is to protect us from foreign invaders who would now disrupt what the rest of the Constitution is all about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: All of the Constitution is written in a way as to preserve, find ways to limit the ability of government to violate the rights of individuals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That the beauty of this Constitution, and again, its connection to the Declaration and tradition, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: What came before it? What came before it was a document, which they all respected, which was the Declaration, which set the context for this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And now the union is there in order to provide for the common defense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Great, because we know that foreign invaders can violate our rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That's what war is about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: To protect us from peace, to establish peace and justice within the country that's based on law, the rule of law, and again, individual liberty.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So to me, when you read the Founders, when you read the Federalist Papers, when you read what they wrote,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: what they're trying to do is figure out the right kind of political system, the right kind of structure to be able to preserve these liberties.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And not all of them had, from my perspective, a perfect understanding of what those liberties entailed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But they were all, even the conservatives that you call conservatives, were all in generally in agreement about the importance of individual liberty and the importance of individual liberty.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Of course, because almost all of these rights are traditional English rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: They exist in the English Bill of Rights, in the English Petition of Rights, in the Existence of Forests.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Of course, of course.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: All of these are traditional.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And what they're trying to do is perfect that. They're trying to take the British system and perfect it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But you keep leaving out that they want to be like England and that they want to have an independent nation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: An independent nation is not a collection of individual liberties.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: An independent nation, the first sentence of the Declaration of Independence is the declaration that there is a collective right,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: that we as a people are breaking the bonds with another people and we're going to take our place, our equal station among the nations of the earth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: For what purpose? The purpose is to protect individual rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And there's no collective right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: No, your argument is completely circular. You're not allowing the possibility that there could be great and decent men that you and I both admire

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: who wanted the independence of their nation, not because that would give individuals liberty,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: but because the independence of their nation was itself a great good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So we clearly disagree on this because I don't think the independence of the nation is a good in and of itself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But do they think it was?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I don't think they did. And this is why they tried so hard not to break from England and why many of them struggled,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: really, really struggled with having a revolution because England was pretty good.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: England was the best. And this is where we should get to the universality of these things because I do think England was the best universally

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and absolutely was the best system out there. And what they would, they struggled to break from England

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: because they didn't view the value of having a nation as the primary.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But what they identified in England is certain flaws in the system that created situations in which their rights were being violated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So they figured the only option in order to secure these rights is to break away from England and secure a nation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Now, I am not an anarchist, as Michael Maus has because we've discussed it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I believe you need nations. You need nations to secure those rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That is, the rights are not, you can't secure those rights without having a nation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But the nation is just a means to an end. The end is the rights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I think that's how the founders understood it. And that's why they created this kind of country.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I think this is a good place to ask about common welfare and cohesion.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Let me say what John Donne wrote that, quote, No man is an island entire of itself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: He went on, Any man's death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And therefore, never send to know for whom the bell tolls. It tolls for thee.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So let's talk about individualism and cohesion, not just at the political level,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: but at a philosophical level for the human condition. What is central?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: What is the role of other humans in our lives? What's the importance of cohesion?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: This is something you've talked about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So, Iran said that the beauty of the founding documents is that they create a cohesive union

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: that protects the individual freedoms. But you have spoken about the value of the union,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: the common welfare, the cohesion in itself.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So can you maybe elaborate on what is the role of cohesion and the collective, not to use that term,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: but multiple humans together, connected in the human condition?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Sure. I keep getting the feeling that you're on and I are actually having a disagreement about empirical reality,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: because I think that enlightenment, rationalist political thought features the individual.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It features the state. There isn't really a nation other than the nation, the people is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: as a collective, is created by the state. And when the state disappears, then the collective disappears.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Now, I think that when conservatives of all stripes look at this kind of thinking,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: that there's the individuals and then there's the state, and there really isn't anything else.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: When they look at that, they say, even before you get to consequences, it's a terrible theory,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: because when we try to understand any field of inquiry, any domain, any subject area,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: when you try to understand it, we try to come up with a small number of concepts

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and of relations among the concepts, which is supposed to be able to explain, to illuminate,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: as much as possible, the important things that are taking place in the domain.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And conservatives look at this, individuals and the state, and they say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: you're missing most of what's going on in politics, also in personal human relations as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But it just doesn't look like a description of human beings. It looks like a completely artificial thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And then conservatives say, well, look, if one wants to adopt this artificial thing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: then the consequences are horrific because you're not describing reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So a conservative reality begins with an empirical view of what are human beings like.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And the first thing you notice about human beings, or at least the first thing I think conservatives notice,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: is that they're sticky, is that they clump, they turn into groups.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And you take any arbitrary collection of human beings and set them to a task, or even just leave them alone,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and they quickly form into groups, and those groups are always structured as hierarchies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: There's this competition within the hierarchy, who's going to be the leader, who's going to be number two.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But everywhere you look in human societies, universally, there are groups.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: The groups compete, and they're structured internally as hierarchies,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and then there are internal competitions for who leads the different groups.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And when we think about scientific explanation, we allow that there are different levels of explanation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: that a macroscopic object like a table, it doesn't have properties that can be directly derived

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: from the properties of the atoms or the molecules or the microfibers that make up the table.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And that's understood, that there's what academic philosophers call emergent properties,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: that when you get up to the level of the table, it has properties, like, you know, that you can't put your fist through it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: which you can't necessarily know just by looking at the atoms alone.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I think conservatives say the same thing is true for political theory, for social theory,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: that looking at an individual human being and thinking about what does that individual human being need,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: which Yaron does very eloquently in his writings,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: but that doesn't tell you what the characteristics are of this hierarchically structured group.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: As soon as you have that, it has its own qualities.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So an example, the question of what holds these groups together, and we need to answer that question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I try to answer it by saying there's such a thing as mutual loyalty.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Mutual loyalty is shorthand for human beings.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Individuals have the capacity to include another individual within their self, within their conception of their self.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: When two people do it, it creates a bond, like a bond between two atoms creates a molecule.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That doesn't mean that they lose their individuality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Within the group, they may still continue competing with one another, but that doesn't mean that there isn't in reality a bond.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That real bond is the stuff of which political events and political history are made,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: is the coming together, the cohesion, and the dissolution of these bonded loyalty groups.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That's the reality of politics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So when I hear these discussions about individuals in the state, I feel like we're missing most of the reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: In order to understand the political reality, we need to understand what makes human beings coherent to groups,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: what makes them dissolve, what makes the groups come apart and end up creating civil wars and that kind of thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I think we also need to know in practice, rival groups do come together and bond.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Basically, when we think about democratic society, we're talking about different groups.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: We can call them tribes or you can come up with a different name, but different tribal groupings with different views,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: they come together to form a nation and they're able to do that even though often they hate each other,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: like we were talking about the American Revolution, and often they hate each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Nevertheless, they're able to come together. Why? How?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That leads us into questions like how does honor, the giving of honor by one group to another,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: how does that increase the mutual loyalty between groups that are still competing with one another?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: All of these questions, I think we have to answer them in order to be able to talk about politics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: I think the first reason why one should approach politics as a conservative rather than as an individualist

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: is because it gives us these theoretical tools to be able to talk about reality,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: which we don't have as long as we keep within the individualist framework.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: As you're talking, the metaphor that's popping up into my mind,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and this is also something that bothers me with theoretical physics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: the metaphor is there's some sense in which this thing is called theories of everything,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: where you try to describe the basic laws of physics, how they interact together,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and once you do, you have a sense that you understand all of reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: In a sense, you do, and that to me is understanding the individual,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: like how the individual behaves in this world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But then you're saying that, hey, you're also forgetting chemistry, biology,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: how all of that actually comes together, the stickiness of molecules and how they build different systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Some systems can kill each other, some systems can flourish,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: some can make pancakes and bananas, and some can make poison and all those kinds of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So we need to consider the full stack of things that are constructed from the fundamental basics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I guess, Yaron, you're saying that, no, you're just like the theoretical physicist.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: It all starts at the bottom.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: You need to preserve the fundamentals of reality,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: which is the individual, like the basic atom of human society is the individual to you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So, yes, the basic unit, the basic moral unit, the basic ethical unit in society is the individual.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And yeah, of course we form groups.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And you can't understand history unless you understand group formation and group motivation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And I have a view about what kind of groups should be formed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And politically, from a political perspective, voluntary ones,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: ones in which we join when we want to join and we can leave when we want to leave.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And ones that help us, and clearly groups help us, pursue whatever it is our goal is ultimately.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So in the pursuit of happiness, there are lots of groups that one wants to form,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: whether it's marriage, whether it's businesses, whether it's sports teams,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: whether it's lots of different groups one wants to form.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: But the question is what is the standard of well-being?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Is it the standard of well-being some algorithm that maximizes the well-being of a group,

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: some utilitarian function?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Is it something that's inherent in the group that we can measure as goodness

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: and to help with the individuals within as long as we can get the group to function well?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: We don't really care about where the individuals are.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: So to me, the goal of creating groups is the well-being of the individual.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And that's why it needs to be voluntary.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And that's why there has to be a way out of those.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Sometimes it's costly. It's not a cheap out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: That's why you should really think about what groups you...

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: And this, you know, on an issue that's very controversial, maybe we can discuss, maybe not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: This is why to me immigration is so important, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256

body.input: Open immigration or free immigration is because that's another group

metadata.title: Podcast: Nationalism Debate: Yaron Brook and Yoram Hazony | Lex Fridman Podcast #256
