metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: We need to have answers for reasoning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: But I think that the core here is that for the first time,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: and I think it is a valuable thing to do,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Although I suspect with GPT, it's scaled more and more.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Sorry to take a step back.

body.input: Can you talk through a story of Dota,

body.input: and so on of training on that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: So with Dota. What is Dota?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Yeah, Dota is a complex video game.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And we started training, we started trying to solve Dota

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: because we felt like this was a step towards the real world

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: relative to other games like Chess or Go, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Those very cerebral games where you just kind of have

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: this board of very discreet moves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Dota starts to be much more continuous time

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that you have this huge variety of different actions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that you have a 45 minute game with all these different units

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: and it's got a lot of messiness to it

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that really hasn't been captured by previous games.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And famously, all of the hard-coded bots for Dota

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: were terrible, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Just impossible to write anything good for it

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: because it's so complex.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And so this seemed like a really good place

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: to push what's the state of the art in reinforcement learning.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And so we started by focusing on the one versus one version

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: of the game and we're able to solve that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: We're able to beat the world champions and the learning,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: the skill curve was this crazy exponential, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And it was like constantly we were just scaling up

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that we were fixing bugs and that you look at the skill curve

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: and it was really a very, very smooth one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: This is actually really interesting to see how that

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: human iteration loop yielded very steady exponential progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And to one side note, first of all,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: it's an exceptionally popular video game.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: The side effect is that there's a lot of incredible

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: human experts at that video game.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: So the benchmark that you're trying to reach is very high.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And the other, can you talk about the approach

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that was used initially and throughout training

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: these agents to play this game?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Yep, and so the approach that we used is self-play.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And so you have two agents that don't know anything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: They battle each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: They discover something a little bit good

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: and now they both know it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And they just get better and better and better

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: without bound.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And that's a really powerful idea, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: That we then went from the one versus one version of the game

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: and you need to do all this coordination

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: and we were able to push the same idea,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: the same self-play to really get to the professional level

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: at the full five versus five version of the game.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And the things I think are really interesting here

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: is that these agents, in some ways,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that gets baked into this agent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And it's not really smart in the sense of a human, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: It's not able to go and learn calculus,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: but it's able to navigate its environment extremely well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: It's able to handle unexpected things in the environment

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that it's never seen before pretty well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And we see the same sort of thing with our Dota bots,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: right, that they're able to, within this game,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: they're able to play against humans,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: which is something that never existed

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: in its evolutionary environment,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And yet it's able to handle it extremely well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And that's something that I think was very surprising to us,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: running with like hundreds of GPUs,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: it was probably about something like hundreds of years

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: of experience going into this bot every single real day.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And so that scale is massive,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: and we start to see very different kinds of behaviors

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: you need real-world experience, you need a body,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: you need grounding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: How are you supposed to reason about any of these things?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: How are you supposed to like even kind of know

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: about smoke and fire and those things

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: if you've never experienced them?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And GPT-2 shows that you can actually go way further

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: than that kind of reasoning would predict.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: So I think that in terms of, do we need consciousness?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Do we need a body?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: It seems the answer is probably not, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: That we could probably just continue to push

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: kind of the systems we have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: They already feel general.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: They're not as competent or as general

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: or able to learn as quickly as an AGI would,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: but you know, they're at least like kind of proto-AGI

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: in some way and they don't need any of those things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Now, let's move to the grand answer,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: which is, you know, if our neural nets conscious already,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: would we ever know, how can we tell, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And you know, here's where the speculation starts

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: to become, you know, at least interesting or fun

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: and maybe a little bit disturbing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: depending on where you take it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: But it certainly seems that when we think about animals,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that there's some continuum of consciousness.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: You know, my cat, I think is conscious in some way, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: You know, not as conscious as a human.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And you could imagine that you could build

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: a little consciousness meter, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: You point at a cat, it gives you a little reading.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Point at a human, it gives you much bigger reading.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Well, what would happen if you pointed one of those

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: at a donor neural net?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And if you're training in this massive simulation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: do the neural nets feel pain?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: You know, it becomes pretty hard to know

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that the answer is no.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And it becomes pretty hard to really think about

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: what that would mean if the answer were yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And it's very possible, you know, for example,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: you could imagine that maybe the reason

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that humans have consciousness is because

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: it's a convenient computational shortcut, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: If you think about it, if you have a being

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that wants to avoid pain, which seems pretty important

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: to survive in this environment and wants to like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: you know, eat food, then that maybe the best way

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: of doing it is to have a being that's conscious, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: That, you know, in order to succeed in the environment,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: you need to have those properties,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: and how are you supposed to implement them?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: And maybe this consciousness's way of doing that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: If that's true, then actually maybe we should expect

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that really competent reinforcement learning agents

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: will also have consciousness.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: But you know, it's a big if, and I think there are

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: a lot of other arguments they can make in other directions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: I think that's a really interesting idea

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: that even GPT-2 has some degree of consciousness.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: That's something, it's actually not as crazy to think about,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: it's useful to think about as we think about

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: what it means to create intelligence of a dog,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: intelligence of a cat, and the intelligence of a human.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: So last question, do you think we will ever fall in love,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: like in the movie Her, with an artificial intelligence system

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: or an artificial intelligence system

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: falling in love with a human?

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: I hope so. If there's any better way to end it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: is on love, so Greg, thanks so much for talking today.

metadata.title: Podcast: Greg Brockman: OpenAI and AGI | Lex Fridman Podcast #17

body.input: Thank you for having me.

body.input: The following is a conversation with Leslie Kaelbling. She is a roboticist and professor

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: at MIT. She is recognized for her work in reinforcement learning, planning, robot navigation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: and several other topics in AI. She won the IJCAI Computers and Thought Award and was the editor-in-chief

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: of the prestigious Journal of Machine Learning Research. This conversation is part of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Artificial Intelligence podcast at MIT and beyond. If you enjoy it, subscribe on YouTube,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: iTunes, or simply connect with me on Twitter at Lex Friedman, spelled F-R-I-D. And now,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: here's my conversation with Leslie Kaelbling. What made me get excited about AI, I can say that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: is I read Gödel Escher Bach when I was in high school. That was pretty formative for me

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: because it exposed the interestingness of primitives and combination and how you can

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: make complex things out of simple parts and ideas of AI and what kinds of programs might

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: generate intelligent behavior. So you first fell in love with AI reasoning logic versus robots?

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Yeah, the robots came because my first job, so I finished an undergraduate degree in philosophy at

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Stanford and was about to finish a master's in computer science. And I got hired at SRI

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: in their AI lab and they were building a robot. It was a kind of a follow-on to shaky, but all

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: the shaky people were not there anymore. And so my job was to try to get this robot to do stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: And that's really kind of what got me interested in robots.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: So maybe taking a small step back, your bachelor's in Stanford in philosophy did a master's in PhD

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: in computer science, but the bachelor's in philosophy. So what was that journey like?

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: What elements of philosophy do you think you bring to your work in computer science?

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: So it's surprisingly relevant. So part of the reason that I didn't do a computer science

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: undergraduate degree was that there wasn't one at Stanford at the time, but that there's part

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: of philosophy. And in fact, Stanford has a special sub major in something called now

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: symbolic systems, which is logic, model theory, formal semantics of natural language. And so

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: that's actually a perfect preparation for work in AI and computer science.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: That's kind of interesting. So if you were interested in artificial intelligence,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: what kind of majors were people even thinking about taking? What is it in your science?

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: So besides philosophies, what were you supposed to do if you were

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: fascinated by the idea of creating intelligence?

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: There weren't enough people who did that for that even to be a conversation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: I think probably philosophy. I mean, it's interesting in my graduating class of

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: undergraduate philosophers, probably maybe slightly less than half went on in computer science,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: slightly less than half went on in law, and like one or two went on in philosophy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: So it was a common kind of connection.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Do you think AI researchers have a role, be part time philosophers, or should they stick

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: to the solid science and engineering without sort of taking the philosophizing tangents?

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: I mean, you work with robots, you think about what it takes to create intelligent beings.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Aren't you the perfect person to think about the big picture philosophy of it all?

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: The parts of philosophy that are closest to AI, I think, or at least the closest to AI that I

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: think about are stuff like belief and knowledge and denotation and that kind of stuff. And that's,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: it's quite formal. And it's like just one step away from the kinds of

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: computer science work that we do kind of routinely.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: I think that there are important questions still about what you can do with a machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: and what you can't and so on. Although at least my personal view is that I'm completely a

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: materialist and I don't think that there's any reason why we can't make a robot be

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: behaviorally indistinguishable from a human. And the question of whether it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: distinguishable internally, whether it's a zombie or not in philosophy terms, I actually don't,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: I don't know. And I don't know if I care too much about that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Right. But there is a philosophical notions, they're mathematical and philosophical because

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: we don't know so much of how difficult it is, how difficult is the perception problem,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: how difficult is the planning problem, how difficult is it to operate in this world

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: successfully because our robots are not currently as successful as human beings in many tasks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: The question about the gap between current robots and human beings borders a little bit on

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: philosophy. You know, the, the expanse of knowledge that's required to operate in this world

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: and the ability to form common sense knowledge, the ability to reason about uncertainty,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: much of the work you've been doing, there's, there's open questions there that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: I don't know, required to activate a certain big picture view.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: To me, that doesn't seem like a philosophical gap at all. To me, it's, there is a big technical gap.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: There's a huge technical gap, but I don't see any reason why it's more than a technical gap.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Perfect. So when you mentioned AI, you mentioned SRI, and maybe can you describe to me when you

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: first fell in love with robotics, with robots or inspired, which, so you mentioned Flaky or

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Shaky, Shaky, Flaky. And what was the robot that first captured your imagination? What's possible?

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Right. Well, so the first robot I worked with was like, Shaky was a robot that the SRI

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: people had built. But by the time I think when I arrived, it was sitting in a corner of somebody's

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: office, dripping hydraulic fluid into a pan. But it's iconic. And really everybody should read the

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Shaky tech report because it has so many good ideas in it. I mean, they invented a star search

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: and symbolic planning and learning macro operators. They had low level kind of configuration space

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: planning for the robot. They had vision. They had all this, the basic ideas of a ton of things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Can you take a step out of this? Shaky have arms. What was the job? What was the goal?

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Shaky was a mobile robot, but it could push objects. And so it would move things around.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: With which actuator? With its self, with its base. Okay, great.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: So it could, but it, and they had painted the baseboards black. So it used, it used vision to

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: localize itself in a map. It detected objects. It could detect objects that were surprising to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: It would plan and replan based on what it saw. It reasoned about whether to look and take pictures.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: I mean, it really had the basics of, of so many of the things that we think about now.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: How did it represent the space around it? So it had representations at a bunch of different

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: levels of abstraction. So it had, I think a kind of an occupancy grid of some sort at the lowest

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: level. At the high level, it was abstract, symbolic kind of rooms and connectivity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: So where does flaky come in? Yeah. Okay. So I showed up at SRI and the,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: we were building a brand new robot. As I said, none of the people from the previous project were

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: kind of there or involved anymore. So we were kind of starting from scratch. And my advisor was Stan

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Rosenstein. He ended up being my thesis advisor and he was motivated by this idea of situated

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: computation or situated automata. And the idea was that the tools of logical reasoning were important,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: but possibly only for the engineers or designers to use in the analysis of a system, but not

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: necessarily to be manipulated in the head of the system itself. Right. So I might use logic to

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: prove a theorem about the behavior of my robot, even if the robot's not using logic in its head

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: to prove theorems. Right. So that was kind of the distinction. And so the idea was to kind of use

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: those principles to make a robot do stuff. But a lot of the basic things we had to kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: On the other hand, maybe a very compact model of the world dynamics plus a planner

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: here lets me compute what action to take too just more slowly. There's no argument to be had. It's

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: just a question of what form of computation is best for us. For the various subproblems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Right. And so learning to do algebra manipulations for some reason, that's probably going to want

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: naturally a different representation than writing a unicycle. The time constraints on the unicycle

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: are serious. The space base is maybe smaller. I don't know. But so I... And there could be the

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: more human size of falling in love, having a relationship. That might be another...

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Yeah, I have no idea. Another style of how to model that. Yeah. Let's first solve the algebra

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: and the object manipulation. What do you think is harder, perception or planning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Perception. That's why I'm planning. Understanding.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Right. That's why. So what do you think is so hard about perception,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: about understanding the world around you? Well, I think the big question

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: is representational. Hugely the question is representational. So perception has made

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: great strides lately, right? And we can classify images and we can play certain kinds of games and

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: predict how to steer the car and all this sort of stuff. I don't think we have a very good idea

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: of what perception should deliver, right? So if you believe in modularity... Okay. There's a very

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: strong view which says we shouldn't build in any modularity. We should make a gigantic neural

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: network, train it end to end to do the thing, and that's the best way forward. And it's hard to argue

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: with that except on a sample complexity basis, right? So you might say, oh, well, if I want to

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: do end to end reinforcement learning on this giant, giant neural network, it's going to take a lot of

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: data and a lot of broken robots and stuff. So then the only answer is to say, okay,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: we have to build something in, build in some structure or some bias. We know from theory of

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: machine learning, the only way to cut down the sample complexity is to kind of cut down, somehow

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: cut down the hypothesis space. You can do that by building in bias. There's all kinds of reasons to

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: think that nature built bias into humans. Convolution is a bias. It's a very strong bias and is a very

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: critical bias. So my own view is that we should look for more things that are like convolution,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: but that address other aspects of reasoning, right? So convolution helps us a lot with a certain kind

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: of spatial reasoning that's quite close to the imaging. I think there's other ideas like that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: maybe some amount of forward search, maybe some notions of abstraction, maybe the notion that

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: objects exist. Actually, I think that's pretty important and a lot of people won't give you that

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: to start with. So almost like a convolution in the semantic object space or some kind of ideas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: That's right. And people are starting to like the graph convolutions are an idea that are related

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: to relational representations. So I think there are, so I've come far afield from perception,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: but I think the thing that's going to make perception the next step is actually understanding

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: better what it should produce. So what are we going to do with the output of it? It's fine when

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: what we're going to do with the output is steer. It's less clear when we're just trying to make

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: one integrated intelligent agent. What should the output of perception be? We have no idea.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: And how should that hook up to the other stuff? We don't know. So I think the pressing question is

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: what kinds of structure can we build in that are like the moral equivalent of convolution

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: that will make a really awesome superstructure that then learning can kind of progress on

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: efficiently? I agree. Very compelling description of actually where we stand with the perception of

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: them. You're teaching a course on embodying intelligence. What do you think it takes to

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: build a robot with human level intelligence? I don't know if we knew we would do it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: If you were to, I mean, okay, so do you think a robot needs to have a self-awareness,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: consciousness, fear of mortality, or is it, is it simpler than that? Or is consciousness a simple

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: thing? Like, do you think about these notions? I don't think much about consciousness. Even most

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: philosophers who care about it will give you that you could have robots that are zombies, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: That behave like humans, but are not conscious. And I at this moment would be happy enough with

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: that. So I'm not really worried one way or the other. So the technical side, you're not thinking

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: of the use of self-awareness. Well, but I okay, but then what is self-awareness mean? I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: that you need to have some part of the system that can observe other parts of the system and

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: tell whether they're working well or not. That seems critical. So does that count as, I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: does that kind of self-awareness or not? Well, it depends on whether you think that there's

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: somebody at home who can articulate whether they're self-aware. But clearly if I have like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: some piece of code that's counting how many times this procedure gets executed,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: that's a kind of self-awareness, right? So there's a big spectrum. It's clear you have to have some

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: of it. Right. You know, we're quite far away on many dimensions, but is there a direction of research

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: that's most compelling to you for, you know, trying to achieve human level intelligence

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: in our robots? Well, to me, I guess the thing that seems most compelling to me at the moment is this

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: question of what to build in and what to learn. And I think that's the most important thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: I think we're missing a bunch of ideas. And people, you know, don't you dare ask me how many years

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: it's going to be until that happens because I won't even participate in the conversation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Because I think we're missing ideas and I don't know how long it's going to take to find them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: So I won't ask you how many years, but maybe I'll ask you

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: when you'll be sufficiently impressed that we've achieved it. So what's a good test of intelligence?

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Do you like the Turing test, the natural language and the robotic space? Is there something

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Do you think about these kinds of problems? No, I resist. I mean, I think all the time that we spend

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: arguing about those kinds of things could be better spent just making the robots work better.

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: or Turing test challenges where everybody kind of gets together and tries to build a better robot

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: Do you see the value of that or can get in the way? I think it can get in the way. I mean,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: some people, many people find it motivating. And so that's good. I find it anti-motivating

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: personally. But I think what, I mean, I think you get an interesting cycle where for a contest,

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: a bunch of smart people get super motivated and they hack their brains out. And much of what gets

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

body.input: done is just hacks, but sometimes really cool things happen. And so I think that's a good

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15

metadata.title: Podcast: Leslie Kaelbling: Reinforcement Learning, Planning, and Robotics | Lex Fridman Podcast #15
