metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So back to the story, the outbreak in the fall.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So now the impact of this virus is significant.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: However, it's a pre-local problem to the point that

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: this is something that we would call a neglected disease

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: because it's not big enough to make the drug design companies

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: to design a new antiviral or a new vaccine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: It's not big enough to generate a lot of grants

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: from the national funding agencies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So does it mean we cannot do anything about it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And so what I did is I taught a bioinformatics class

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: in Worcester Polytechnic Institute,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: and we are very much a problem learning institution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So I thought that that would be a perfect project for the class.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: It's an ongoing case study.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So we essentially designed a study where we tried to use

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: bioinformatics to understand as much as possible about this virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And a very substantial portion of the study was to understand

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: the structures of the proteins, to understand how they interact

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: with each other and with the host proteins,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: try to understand the evolution of this virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So obviously, a very important question,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: where it will evolve further, how it happened here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So we did all these projects, and now I'm trying to put them

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: into a paper where all these undergraduate students will be co-authors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: But essentially, the projects were finished right about mid-December.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And a couple of weeks later, I heard about this mysterious new virus

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: that was discovered and was reported in Wuhan province.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And immediately, I thought that, well, we just did that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Can't we do the same thing with this virus?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And so we started waiting for the genome to be released,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: because that's essentially the first piece of information that is critical.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Once you have the genome sequence, you can start doing a lot using bioinformatics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: When you say genome sequence, that's referring to the sequence of letters that make up the RNA?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: The sequence that make up the entire information encoded in the protein.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So that includes all 29 genes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: What are genes? What's the encoding of information?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So genes essentially is a basic functional unit that we can consider.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So each gene in the virus would correspond to a protein.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So gene by itself doesn't do its function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: It needs to be converted or translated into the protein

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: that will become the actual functional unit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Like you said, the printer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So we need the printer for that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Okay. So the first step is to figure out the genome,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: the sequence of things that will be then used for printing the protein.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So then the next step, so once we have this,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: and so we use the existing information about SARS,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: because the SARS genomics has been done in abundance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So we have different strains of SARS and actually other related coronaviruses, MERS, the bat coronavirus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And we started by identifying the potential genes, because right now it's just a sequence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So it's a sequence that is roughly less than 30,000 nucleotide long.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Just a raw sequence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: It's a raw sequence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: No other information really.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And we now need to define the boundaries of the genes

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: that would then be used to identify the proteins and protein structures.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: How hard is that problem?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: It's pretty straightforward,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: because we use the existing information about SARS proteins and SARS genes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So once again, you kind of...

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: We are relying on the... Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And then once we get there,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: this is where sort of the first more traditional bioinformatics step begins.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: We're trying to use these protein sequences and get the 3D information about those proteins.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So this is where we are relying heavily on the structure information,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: specifically from the protein data bank that we were talking about.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And here you're looking for similar proteins.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Yes. So the concept that we are operating when we do this kind of modeling,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: it's called homology or template-based modeling.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So essentially using the concept that if you have two sequences that are similar in terms of the letters,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: the structures of the sequences are expected to be similar as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And this is at the micro, at the very local scale and...

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: At the scale of the whole protein.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: The whole protein.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So actually, of course, the devil is in the details,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: and this is why we need actually pre-sophisticated modeling tools to do so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Once we get these structures of the individual proteins,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: we try to see whether or not these proteins act alone

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: or they have to be forming protein complexes in order to perform this function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And again, so this is sort of the next level of the modeling

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: because now you need to understand how proteins interact.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And it could be the case that the protein interacts with itself and makes sort of a multimeric complex.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: The same protein just repeated multiple times,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: and we have quite a few such proteins in SARS-CoV-2,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: specifically spike protein needs three copies to function,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: envelope protein needs five copies to function,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: and there are some other multimeric complexes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: That's what you mean by interacting with itself and you see multiple copies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So how do you make a good guess whether something's going to interact?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Well, again, so there are two approaches.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: One is look at the previously solved complexes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Now we're looking not at the individual structures, but the structures of the whole complex.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Complexes of multiple proteins.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Yes, so it's a bunch of proteins essentially glued together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And when you say glued, that's the interaction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: That's the interaction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So there are different forces, different sort of physical forces behind this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Sorry to keep asking dumb questions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: but is the interaction fundamentally structural or is it functional in the way you're thinking about it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: That's actually a very good way to ask this question

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: because turns out that the interaction is structural,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: but in the way it forms the structure, it actually also carries out the function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So interaction is often needed to carry out very specific function or protein.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: But in terms of on the reverse side,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: figuring out you're really starting at the structure before you figure out the function.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So there's a beautiful figure too in the paper of all the different proteins that make up,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: able to figure out the make up the novel coronavirus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: What are we looking at?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So these are like, that's through the step two that you mentioned,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: when you try to guess at the possible proteins, that's what you're going to get is these blue cyan blobs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Yes. So those are the individual proteins for which we have at least some information from the previous studies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So there is advantage and disadvantage of using previous studies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: The biggest disadvantage is that we may not necessarily have the coverage of all 29 proteins.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: However, the biggest advantage is that the accuracy in which we can model these proteins is very high,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: much higher compared to ab initio methods that do not use any template information.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: But nevertheless, this figure also has such a beautiful, I love these pictures so much,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: it has like the pink parts, which are the parts that are different.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So the difference you find is on the 2D sequence, and then you try to infer what that will look like on the 3D.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So the difference actually is on 1D sequence.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: 1D, sorry, not 2D, right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And so this is one of these first questions that we tried to answer is that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: well, if you take this new virus and you take the closest relatives,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: which are SARS and a couple of bad coronavirus strains,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: they are already the closest relatives that we are aware of.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Now, what are the difference between this virus and its close relatives?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And if you look, typically when you take a sequence, those differences could be quite far away from each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So what 3D structure makes those difference to do, very often they tend to cluster together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And over sudden, the differences that may look completely unrelated actually relate to each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And sometimes they are there because they attack the functional site.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So they are there because this is the functional site that is highly mutated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So that's a computational approach to figuring something out.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And when it comes together like that, that's kind of a nice clean indication that there's something,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: this could be actually indicative of what's happening.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Yes. So we need this information.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And the 3D structure gives us just a very intuitive way to look at this information.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And then start asking questions such as, so this place of this protein that is highly mutated,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: is it the functional part of the protein?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So we will try now to functionally inform this 3D structure.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: so the first thing that you start seeing, you look at patterns.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Well, so one of the most interesting findings we had was the fact that the binding sites on the viral surfaces

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: that get targeted by the known small molecules, they were pretty much not affected at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And so that means that the same small drugs or small drug-like compounds can be efficient for the new coronavirus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So this all actually maps to the drug compounds too.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So you're actually mapping out what old stuff is going to work on this thing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: and then possibilities for new stuff to work by mapping out that things have mutated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Yes. So we essentially know which parts behave differently and which parts are likely to behave similar.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And again, of course, all our predictions need to be validated by experiments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: But hopefully that sort of helps us to delineate the regions of this virus that can be promising in terms of the drug discovery.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: You kind of mentioned this already, but maybe you can elaborate.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So how different from the structural and functional perspective does the new coronavirus appear to be relative to SARS?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: We now are trying to understand the overall structural characteristics of this virus,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: because that's our next step, trying to model the single viral particle of this virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So that means you have the individual proteins. Like you said, you have to figure out what their interaction is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Is that where this graph kind of interactome?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So the interactome is essentially our prediction on the potential interactions,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: some of them that we already deciphered from the structural knowledge,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: but some of them that are essentially deciphered from the knowledge of the existing interactions

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: that people previously obtained for SARS, for MERS, or other related viruses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Is there kind of interactomes? Am I pronouncing that correctly by the way?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Yeah, interactome.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Are those already converged towards for SARS?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: I think there are a couple of papers that now investigate the large-scale sets of interactions between the new SARS and its host.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And so I think that's an ongoing study.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And the success of that, the result would be an interactome.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And so when you say not trying to figure out the entire particle, the entire thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So structure, right? So what this viral particle looks like, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So as I said, the surface of it is an envelope, which is essentially a so-called lipid bilayer with proteins integrated into the surface.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So an average particle is around 18 nanometers, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So this particle can have about 50 to 100 spike proteins.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So at least we suspect it, and based on the micrographs images, it's very comparable to MHV virus in mice and SARS virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Micrographs are actual pictures of the actual...

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Okay, so these are models.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: These are the actual images, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: What are they? Sorry for the tangents, but what are these things?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So when you look on the Internet, the models and the pictures are... and the models you have here are just gorgeous and beautiful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: When you actually take pictures of them with a micrograph, what do we look...

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Well, they typically are not perfect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So most of the images that you see now is the sphere with those spikes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Do you actually see the spikes?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Yes, you do see the spikes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And now, our collaborators for Texas A&M University, Benjamin Newman, he actually...

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: In the recent paper about SARS, he proposed, and there's some actually evidence behind it, that the particle is not a sphere,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: but it actually is an elongated ellipsoid-like particle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So that's what we are trying to incorporate into our model.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And if you look at the actual micrographs, you see that those particles are not symmetric.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So there are some of them. And of course, it could be due to the treatment of the material.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: It could be due to some noise in the imaging.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So there's a lot of uncertainty in all this. So structurally figuring out the entire part...

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: By the way, again, sorry for the tangents, but why the term particle? Or is it just something that's stuck?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: It's a single... We call it the virion. So virion particle, it's essentially a single virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Single virus, but it just feels like...

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Because particle to me, from the physics perspective, feels like the most basic unit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Because there seems to be so much going on inside the virus. It doesn't feel like a particle to me.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Yeah, it's probably... I think virion is a good way to call it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Okay, so trying to figure out the entirety of the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Yes. So virion has 50 to 100 trimer spikes. It has roughly 200 to 400 membrane protein dimers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And those are arranged in the very nice lattice, so you can actually see it's like a carpet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: On the surface again.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Exactly, on the surface. And occasionally you also see this envelope protein inside.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Is that the one we don't know what it does?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Exactly. The one that forms the pentamer, this very nice pentameric ring.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And so this is what we're trying to put now all our knowledge together

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: and see whether we can actually generate this overall virion model

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: with an idea to understand, well, first of all, to understand how it looks like,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: how far it is from those images that were generated. But the implications are

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: there is a potential for the nanoparticle design that will mimic this virion particle.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Is the process of nanoparticle design meaning artificially designing something that looks similar?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Yes. The one that can potentially compete with the actual virion particles

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: and therefore reduce the effect of the infection.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So is this the idea of like what is a vaccine?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So there are two ways of essentially treating and in the case of vaccine is preventing the infection.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So vaccine is a way to train our immune system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So our immune system becomes aware of this new danger and therefore is capable of generating the antibodies

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: then will essentially bind to the spike proteins because that's the main target for the vaccines design

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: and block its functioning. If you have the spike with the antibody on top, it can no longer interact with AC2 receptor.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So the process of designing a vaccine then is you have to understand enough about the structure of the virus itself

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: to be able to create an artificial particle?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Well, I mean, so the nanoparticle is a very exciting and new research.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So there are already established ways to make vaccines and there are several different ones.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So there is one where essentially the virus gets through the cell culture multiple times.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So it becomes essentially adjusted to the specific embryonic cell and as a result becomes less compatible with the host human cells.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So therefore it's sort of the idea of the live vaccine where the particles are there, but they are not so efficient.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So they cannot replicate as rapidly as before the vaccine and they can be introduced to the immune system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: The immune system will learn and the person who gets this vaccine won't get sick or will have mild symptoms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So then there is sort of different types of the way to introduce the non-functional parts of this virus

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: or the virus where some of the information is stripped down.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: For example, the virus with no genetic material, so with no RNA genome.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Exactly. So it cannot replicate. It cannot essentially perform most of its functions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: This is fascinating. What is the biggest hurdle to design one of these, to arrive at one of these?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Is it the work that you're doing in the fundamental understanding of this new virus or is it from our perspective complicated world of experimental validation

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: and sort of going through the whole process of showing this is actually going to work with FDA approval, all that kind of stuff?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: I think it's both. I mean, our understanding of the molecular mechanisms will allow us to design,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: to have more efficient designs of the vaccines. However, once you design the vaccine, it needs to be tested.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: But when you look at the 18 months and the different projections, it seems like an exceptionally, historically speaking,

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: maybe you can correct me, but even 18 months seems like a very accelerated timeline.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: It is. I mean, I remember reading in a book about some previous vaccines that it could take up to 10 years to design

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: and properly test a vaccine before its mass production. So yeah, everything is accelerated these days.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: I mean, for better, for worse, but we definitely need that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Well, especially with the coronavirus, I mean, the scientific community is really stepping up and working together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: The collaborative aspect is really interesting. You mentioned, so the vaccine is one, and then there's antivirals, antiviral drugs.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So antiviral drugs, so where, you know, vaccines are typically needed to prevent the infection, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: But once you have an infection, one, you know, so what we try to do, we try to stop it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So we try to stop virus from functioning. And so the antiviral drugs are designed to block some critical functioning of the proteins from the virus.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So there are a number of interesting candidates. And I think, you know, if you ask me, I think Remdesivir is perhaps the most promising.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: It has been shown to be, you know, an efficient and effective antiviral for SARS.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Originally, it was the antiviral drug developed for a completely different virus, I think, for Ebola and Marburg.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: At a high level, do you know how it works?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So it tries to mimic one of the nucleotides in RNA, and essentially that stops the replication.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So messes, I guess that's what, so antiviral drugs mess with some aspect of this process.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So, you know, so essentially we try to stop certain functions of the virus. There are some other ones, you know, that are designed to inhibit the protease, the thing that clips protein sequences.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: There is one that was originally designed for malaria, which is a bacterial disease.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: This is so cool. But that's exactly where your work steps in, is you're figuring out the functional and the structure of these different, so like providing candidates for where drugs can plug in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Exactly. Well, yes, because, you know, one thing that we don't know is whether or not, so let's say we have a perfect drug candidate that is efficient against SARS and against MERS.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Now, is it going to be efficient against new SARS-CoV-2?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: We don't know that, and there are multiple aspects that can affect this efficiency.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So, for instance, if the binding site, so the part of the protein where this ligand gets attached, if this site is mutated, then the ligand may not be attachable to this part any longer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And, you know, our work and the work of other bioinformatics groups, you know, essentially are trying to understand whether or not that will be the case.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And it looks like for the ligands that we looked at, the ligand binding sites are pretty much intact, which is very promising.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So if we could just like zoom out for a second. Are you optimistic?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So there's two, well, there's three possible ends to the coronavirus pandemic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So one is there's, or drugs or vaccines get figured out very quickly, probably drugs first.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: The other is the pandemic runs its course for this wave, at least.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And then the third is, you know, things go much worse in some in some dark, bad, very bad direction.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Do you see, let's focus on the first two.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Do you see the anti drugs of the work you're doing being relevant for us right now?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: In us stopping the pandemic, or do you hope that the pandemic will run its course?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: So the social distancing, things like wearing masks, all those discussions that we're having will be the method with which we fight coronavirus in the short term.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Or do you think that it'll have to be anti viral drugs?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: I think I think antivirals would be, I would view that as the at least the short term solution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: I see more and more cases in the news of those new drug candidates being administered in hospitals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And I mean, this is right now the best what we have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Or do we need it to reopen the economy?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: I mean, we definitely need it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: I cannot speculate on how that will affect reopening of the economy because we are, you know, we are kind of deep in into the pandemic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And it's not just the states, it's also worldwide.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Of course, there is also the possibility of the second wave, as you mentioned.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: And this is why we need to be super careful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: We need to follow all the precautions that the doctors tell us to do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Are you worried about the mutation of the virus?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: It's, of course, a real possibility.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Now, how to what extent this virus can mutate?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: It's an open question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: I mean, we know that it is able to mutate, to jump from one species to another and to become transmittable between humans.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Right. So, will it, you know, so let's imagine that we have the new antiviral.

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90

body.input: Will this virus become eventually resistant to this antiviral?

metadata.title: Podcast: Dmitry Korkin: Computational Biology of Coronavirus | Lex Fridman Podcast #90
