metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: but it is preserved.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: Got it, okay.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: All right, that's beautiful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So then the electron versus light distinction

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and why are electrons good at computation

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and light good at communication?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: Yes, this is, there's a lot that goes into it, I guess,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: but just try to speak to the simplest part of it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: Electrons interact strongly with one another.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: They're charged particles.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So if I pile a bunch of them over here,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: they're feeling a certain amount of force

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and they wanna move somewhere else.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: They're strongly interactive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: You can also get them to sit still.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: An electron has a mass,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: so you can cause it to be spatially localized.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So for computation, that's useful

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: because now I can make these little devices

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: that put a bunch of electrons over here

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and then I change the state of a gate

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: like I've been describing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: put a different voltage on this gate

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and now I move the electrons over here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: Now they're sitting somewhere else.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: I have a physical mechanism

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: with which I can represent information.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: It's spatially localized and I have knobs

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: that I can adjust to change where those electrons are

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: or what they're doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: Light by contrast, photons of light,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: which are the discrete packets of energy

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: that were identified by Einstein,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: they do not interact with each other,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: especially at low light levels.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: If you're in a medium and you have a bright high light level,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: you can get them to interact with each other

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: through the interaction with that medium that they're in,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: but that's a little bit more exotic.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: And for the purposes of this conversation,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: we can assume that photons don't interact with each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So if you have a bunch of them

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: all propagating in the same direction,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: they don't interfere with each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: If I wanna send, if I have a communication channel

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and I put one more photon on it,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: it doesn't screw up with those other,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: it doesn't change what those other ones were doing at all.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So that's really useful for communication

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: because that means you can sort of allow

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: a lot of these photons to flow

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: without disruption of each other

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and they can branch really easily and things like that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: but it's not good for computation

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: because it's very hard for this packet of light

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: to change what this packet of light is doing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: They pass right through each other.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So in computation, you want to change information

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and if photons don't interact with each other,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: it's difficult to get them to change

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: the information represented by the others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So that's the fundamental difference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: Is there also something about the way they travel

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: through different materials

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: or is that just a particular engineering?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: No, it's not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: That's deep physics, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So this gets back to electrons interact with each other

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and photons don't.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So say I'm trying to get a packet of information

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: from me to you and we have a wire going between us.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: In order for me to send electrons across that wire,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: I first have to raise the voltage at my end of the wire

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and that means putting a bunch of charges on it

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and then that charge packet has to propagate along the wire

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and it has to get all the way over to you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: That wire is gonna have something that's called capacitance,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: which basically tells you how much charge you need

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: to put on the wire in order to raise the voltage on it

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and the capacitance is gonna be proportional

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: to the length of the wire.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So the longer the length of the wire is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: the more charge I have to put on it

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and the energy required to charge up that line

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and move those electrons to you

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: is also proportional to the capacitance

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and goes as the voltage squared.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So you get this huge penalty if you wanna send electrons

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: across a wire over appreciable distances.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So distance is an important thing here

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: when you're doing communication.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: Distance is an important thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So is the number of connections I'm trying to make.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: Me to you, okay, one, that's not so bad.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: If I want to now send it to 10,000 other friends,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: then all of those wires are adding tons

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: of extra capacitance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: Now, not only does it take forever

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: to put the charge on that wire

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and raise the voltage on all those lines,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: but it takes a ton of power.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: And the number 10,000 is not randomly chosen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: That's roughly how many connections

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: each neuron in your brain makes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So a neuron in your brain needs to send 10,000 messages

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: every time it has something to say.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: You can't do that if you're trying to drive electrons

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: from here to 10,000 different places.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: The brain does it in a slightly different way,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: which we can discuss.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: How can light achieve the 10,000 connections

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and why is it better in terms of the energy use

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: required to use light for the communication

body.input: of the 10,000 connections?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: Right, right.

body.input: So now instead of trying to send electrons for me to you,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: I'm trying to send photons.

body.input: So I can make what's called a wave guide,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: or silicon on a chip.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: And I just have to inject photons into that wave guide

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and independent of how long it is,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: independent of how many different connections I'm making,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: it doesn't change the voltage or anything like that

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: that I have to raise up on the wire.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So if I have one more connection,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: if I add additional connections,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: I need to add more light to the wave guide

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: because those photons need to split

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: and go to different paths.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: That makes sense, but I don't have a capacitive penalty.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: Sometimes these are called wiring parasitics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: There are no parasitics associated with light

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: in that same sense.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: Well, this might be a dumb question,

body.input: Is it the polymer stuff you were talking about

body.input: Like how do you catch a photon?

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: There's a lot of ways to catch a photon.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: It's not a dumb question.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: It's a deep and important question

body.input: that basically defines a lot of the work

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: that goes on in our group at NIST.

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: One of my group leaders, Sehwoonam,

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: has built his career around these superconducting

metadata.title: Podcast: Jeffrey Shainline: Neuromorphic Computing and Optoelectronic Intelligence | Lex Fridman Podcast #225

body.input: So if you're going to try to sort of reach a lower limit

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: So the IBM 650 was this machine that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: well, it didn't fill a room, but it was big and noisy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But when I first saw it, it was through a window,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: and there were just a lot of lights flashing on it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And I was a freshman.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: I had a job with the statistics group,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: and I was supposed to punch cards for data

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: and then sort them on another machine,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: but they got this new computer, came in,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: and it had interesting lights.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Okay, so, well, but I had a key to the building,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: so I could get in and look at it and got a manual for it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And my first experience was based on the fact

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: that I could punch cards, basically,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: which is a big thing for the deal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But the IBM 650 was big in size,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: but incredibly small in power in memory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: It had 2,000 words of memory,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And it would do, to add two numbers together,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: you could probably expect that would take,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: So pretty fast.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: The memory is the constraint.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: The memory is the problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And you had to wait, I don't know, five cycle times.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: If you have an instruction in one position on the drum,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: then it would be ready to read the data for the instruction

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: and go three notches.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: The drum is 50 cycles around,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: and you go three cycles, and you can get the data,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: and then you can go another three cycles

body.input: and get to your next instruction,

body.input: if the instruction is there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Otherwise, you spin until you get to the right place.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And we had no random access memory whatsoever

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: until my senior year.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: which were priceless.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Could you have predicted the future

body.input: 60 years later of computing from then?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: No, in fact, the hardest question I was ever asked was,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: In other words, the interviewer asked me,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: she said, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: what about computing has surprised you?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: You know, and immediately I ran,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: I rattled off a couple of dozen things,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: and then she said, okay, so what didn't surprise?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And I tried for five minutes to think of something

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: that I would have predicted, and I couldn't.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But let me say that this machine, I didn't know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: well, there wasn't much else in the world at that time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: The 650 was the first machine

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: that there were more than a thousand of ever.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Before that, there was each machine,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: there might be a half a dozen examples, maybe.

body.input: The first mass market, mass produced.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: It's true that I think there's something

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But it didn't look right on the page.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: The number two was particularly ugly.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: I couldn't stand any page that had a two in its page number.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And I was expecting that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: I spent all this time making measurements and I had looked at stuff in different ways.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And I had great technology, but I wasn't done.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: I had to retune the whole thing after 1961.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Has it ever made you happy, finally?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Oh, yes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Or is it a.8?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: No, and so many books have come out that would never have been written without this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: It's just a joy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But now, all these pages that are sitting up there, if I didn't like them, I would change them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Nobody else has this ability.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: They have to stick with what I gave them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: So in terms of the other side of it, there's the typography, so the look of the type and the curves and the lines.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: What about the spacing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: What about the spacing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: The white space.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: It seems like you could be a little bit more systematic about the layout or technical.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Oh, yeah, you can always go further.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: I didn't stop at.8.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: I stopped at about.98.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: It seems like you're not following your own rule for happiness.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: No, no, no.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Of course, there's this Japanese word, wabi-sabi, or something, where the most beautiful works of art are those that have flaws,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: but then the person who perceives them adds their own appreciation, and that gives the viewer more satisfaction, or so on.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But no, no.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: With typography, I wanted it to look as good as I could in the vast majority of cases.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And then when it doesn't, then I say, okay, that's 2% more work for the author.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But I didn't want to say that my job was to get 200% and take all the work away from the author.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: That's what I meant by that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: So if you were to venture a guess, how much of the nature of reality do you think we humans understand?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: You mentioned you appreciate mystery.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: How much of the world about us is shrouded in mystery?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: If you were to put a number on it, what percent of it all do we understand?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: How many leading zeros? 0.00? I don't know. I think it's infinitesimal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: How do we think about that, and what do we do about that? Do we continue, one step at a time?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Yeah, we muddle through. We do our best. We realize that nobody's perfect.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And we try to keep advancing, but we don't spend time saying we're not there, we're not all the way to the end.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Some mathematicians that would be in the office next to me when I was in the math department,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: they would never think about anything smaller than countable infinity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And we intersected that countable infinity because I rarely got up to countable infinity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: I was always talking about finite stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But even limiting to finite stuff, which the universe might be,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: there's no way to really know whether the universe isn't just made out of capital N,

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: whatever units you want to call them, quarks or whatever, where capital N is some finite number.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: All of the numbers that are comprehensible are still way smaller than almost all finite numbers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: I got this one paper called Supernatural Numbers, where I guess you probably ran into something called Knuth arrow notation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Did you ever run into that? Anyway, so you take the number, I think it's like, and I called it Super K.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: I named it after myself, but arrow notation is something like 10 and then four arrows and a three or something like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Now, the arrow notation, if you have no arrows, that means multiplication.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: X, Y means X times X times X times X, Y times.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: If you have one arrow, that means exponentiation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: So X one arrow Y means X to the X to the X to the X to the Y times.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: So I found out, by the way, that this notation was invented by a guy in 1830.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And he was one of the English nobility who spent his time thinking about stuff like this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And it was exactly the same concept that I used arrows and he used a slightly different notation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But anyway, this and then this Ackerman's function is based on the same kind of ideas.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But Ackerman was 1920s. But anyway, you've got this number, 10 quadruple arrow three.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: So that says, well, we take 10 to the 10th. How many times do we do that?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Oh, 10 double arrow two times or something. I mean, how tall is that stack?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But then we do that again, because that was only 10 quadruple arrow two.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: It gets way beyond comprehension.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But it's so small compared to what finite numbers really are, because I want to use four arrows and a 10 and a 3.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Let's have that many number arrows.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: The boundary between infinite and finite is incomprehensible for us humans anyway.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Infinity is a useful way for us to think about extremely large things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: And we can manipulate it, but we can never know that the universe is actually anywhere near that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: So I realize how little we know.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: But we found an awful lot of things that are too hard for any one person to know, even in our small universe.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Yeah, and we did pretty good. So when you go up to heaven and meet God and get to ask one question that would get answered, what question would you ask?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: What kind of browser do you have up here?

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: I don't think it's meaningful to ask this question, but I certainly hope we had good internet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Okay. On that note, that's beautiful actually. Don, thank you so much. It was a huge honor to talk to you. I really appreciate it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Well, thanks for the gamut of questions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Yeah, it was fun.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Now, let me leave you with some words of wisdom from Donald Knuth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: We should continually be striving to transform every art into a science. And in the process, we advance the art.

metadata.title: Podcast: Donald Knuth: Algorithms, Complexity, and The Art of Computer Programming | Lex Fridman Podcast #62

body.input: Thank you for listening and hope to see you next time.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: And it has a sensor that measures the system's deviation

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: from that set point and an effector

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: that can be parameterized by the controller.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: So the controller tells the effector to do a certain thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: And the goal is to reduce the distance

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: between the set point and the current value of the system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: And there's an environment

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: which disturbs the regulated system,

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: which brings it away from that set point.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: So simplest case is the thermostat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: And if you want to minimize the set point deviation

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: So you need to make a model of what's going to happen when.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: consciousness, so to speak.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: We get some consciousness above our pay grade,

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: maybe, if we have some suffering early in our life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: Most of the interesting people had trauma

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: early on in their childhood.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: And trauma means that you are suffering

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: an injury for which the system is not prepared, which it cannot

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: deal with, which it cannot insulate itself from.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: So something breaks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: And this means that the behavior of the system

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: is permanently disturbed in the way that some mismatch exists

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: now in the regulation, that just by following your impulses,

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: by following the pain in the direction which it hurts,

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: the situation doesn't improve but get worse.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: And so what needs to happen is that you grow up.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: And that's part that is grown up is

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: able to deal with the part that is stuck in this earlier phase.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: So it leads to growth, adding extra layers to your cognition.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: Let me ask you then, because I got to stick on suffering,

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: the ethics of the whole thing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: So not our consciousness, but the consciousness of others.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: You've tweeted, one of my biggest fears

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: is that insects could be conscious.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: The amount of suffering on Earth would be unthinkable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: So when we think of other conscious beings,

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: is suffering a property of consciousness

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: that we're most concerned about?

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: So I'm still thinking about robots,

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: how to make sense of other non-human things that

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: appear to have the depth of experience that humans have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: And to me, that means consciousness

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: and the darkest side of that, which is suffering,

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: the capacity to suffer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: And so I started thinking, how much responsibility

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: do we have for those other conscious beings?

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: That's where the definition of consciousness

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: becomes most urgent.

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: Like having to come up with the definition of consciousness

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: becomes most urgent, is who should we

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: and should we not be torturing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Joscha Bach: Nature of Reality, Dreams, and Consciousness | Lex Fridman Podcast #212

body.input: There's no general answer to this.
